weeks.title: Your second way out
weeks.why: Fire drills happen at random twice a year, so walk your route before one surprises you.

mission.t: Walk to your second-nearest stairwell and back
mission.detail: Find it on the posted floor plan first, then walk it, so a smoke-filled stairwell can't leave you stuck.

huddle.scenario: The alarm sounds and the stairwell most of us use is filling with smoke.
huddle.q1: Which stairwell would each of us use instead, and how do we get there?
huddle.q2: If one of us were on crutches next month, what would our plan be?

weeks.title: Dark evenings, late nights
weeks.why: As evenings get dark earlier, more of us leave ESQ after dark.

mission.t: Find the After-Hours Logbook at the Security desk
mission.detail: Signing it, calling 780-428-1541 or emailing Security tells them you're in the building.

huddle.scenario: A teammate is staying until 9 PM to finish a deadline, alone on the floor.
huddle.q1: How do we make sure Security knows they're here, and that they've left?
huddle.q2: When would you book a Safe Walk, and what stops people from asking for one?

weeks.title: Winter weather ready
weeks.why: Winter storms, freezing rain and power cuts can arrive with little warning.

mission.t: Pick your take-cover spot away from the windows
mission.detail: A stairwell or sturdy table away from exterior walls is where you'd go if high winds threaten the glass.

huddle.scenario: Freezing rain is forecast for late afternoon, and two of us drive in from out of town.
huddle.q1: What would we do if the roads became dangerous before the end of the day?
huddle.q2: Do we all have the MyUAlberta app installed with notifications on?

weeks.title: Hazard hunt
weeks.why: Before the season's events and decorations go up, check your spaces for fire and trip hazards.

mission.t: Check 18 inches of clearance under one sprinkler head
mission.detail: Look up in a storage area or meeting room, move anything stored too close, and report what you can't fix to ClikFix.

huddle.scenario: Someone wants to hang a banner from the meeting room's sprinkler pipe and bring in a space heater for the party.
huddle.q1: What would we say in the moment, and who would say it?
huddle.q2: What's one hazard in our space we've all stopped noticing?

weeks.title: Near misses count
weeks.why: Icy sidewalks and wet entryways bring a season of slips and close calls.

mission.t: Walk your floor and note one unsafe condition
mission.detail: Report it the same day: ClikFix for ESQ building repairs, and a U of A incident report if it was a near miss.

huddle.scenario: Someone slipped on melted snow by the entrance, caught the railing, and said, "No harm done."
huddle.q1: Would you report it? What gets in the way of reporting near misses?
huddle.q2: How can we make reporting the normal thing to do on our team?

weeks.title: First on scene
weeks.why: Busy workshop season brings more visitors who don't know ESQ into our rooms.

mission.t: Find the AED nearest your desk
mission.detail: Check your floor's listing or the red heart on the floor plan, then walk there once so you know the way.

huddle.scenario: A participant collapses during a workshop in a room we've booked.
huddle.q1: Who calls 911, who calls ESQ Security, and who meets the responders?
huddle.q2: If someone spotted smoke instead, what would our first three moves be?

weeks.title: Speak-up week
weeks.why: Mental health awareness campaigns are a good prompt to check how safe it feels to speak up.

mission.t: Thank a colleague, in person, for flagging a problem
mission.detail: Be specific about what they raised; it shows that raising concerns is welcome here.

huddle.scenario: A teammate admits she sent a workshop invite with the wrong date to 200 people.
huddle.q1: What response would make her, and the rest of us, flag the next mistake early?
huddle.q2: Is there anything that makes it harder to raise concerns on our team?

weeks.title: The coffee code
weeks.why: End-of-term visitor traffic is a good time to rehearse calling Security quietly.

mission.t: Find the help station nearest your desk or meeting room
mission.detail: Help stations connect straight to ESQ Security; if your floor has none listed, note the nearest phone instead.

huddle.scenario: A visitor at reception is getting louder and is standing between our colleague and the door.
huddle.q1: What exactly would you say to Security, and in what order?
huddle.q2: Who else on the floor needs to know, and how would we warn them quietly?

questions.q: You're running a meeting on the 3rd floor when the fire alarm sounds. Someone says it's probably the twice-yearly drill and suggests finishing the agenda first. What do you do?

opts.t: Finish the current item quickly, then leave if the alarm is still going
opts.fb: Drills are random, and you can't tell a drill from a real alarm. Every minute you stay is a minute you may not have.

opts.t: End the meeting and evacuate now
opts.fb: Self-evacuation is ESQ's primary response to any alarm. Fire drills happen twice a year at random, so treat every alarm as real.

opts.t: Call the Security desk to ask whether it's a drill before anyone leaves
opts.fb: That delays everyone and ties up Security's line during an emergency. You can't tell a drill from a real alarm, so leave now.

questions.src: ESQ Emergency Procedures 2025 — Introduction; Mock Emergency Drills

questions.q: The alarm sounds while you're on the 2nd floor, right beside the escalators. The nearest emergency stairwell is a short walk away. How do you go down?

opts.t: Ride the escalator, since it's closer and moves faster
opts.fb: Escalators aren't an evacuation route. The procedure is clear: don't use elevators or escalators to evacuate.

opts.t: Wait at the elevators with a colleague who's already pressed the button
opts.fb: During an alarm the elevator touch pads go blank and the elevators return to the main floor, so they won't take you anywhere.

opts.t: Walk to the nearest emergency stairwell
opts.fb: ESQ has 8 emergency stairwells to spread out the traffic. Let the stairwell door close behind you.

questions.src: ESQ Emergency Procedures 2025 — Alarm Response (Tenants); Life Safety Systems

questions.q: A new colleague presses the push bar on a stairwell door, hears an electronic tone, and lets go. "It's alarmed, we can't use this one," they say. What do you tell them?

opts.t: Try the next stairwell, since this door seems to be locked
opts.fb: The door isn't locked out. It has a built-in delay, so walking to another stairwell wastes time.

opts.t: Keep pressing the bar for 15 seconds and it will unlock
opts.fb: The tone is normal and nothing to worry about. Hold the bar the full 15 seconds and the door releases.

opts.t: Wait here for the Floor Warden to come and open it
opts.fb: Floor Wardens direct people to exits, but they don't need to unlock this door. Hold the push bar for 15 seconds.

questions.src: ESQ Emergency Procedures 2025 — Alarm Response (Tenants), step 4

questions.q: On the way down the stairwell, you see the stairs keep going below the main floor toward the concourse and the LRT. Your train home leaves from that station. Where do you leave the building?

opts.t: At the main floor (ground level) exit
opts.fb: All stairways continue to the concourse, but you exit at the main floor only. Then head to the muster point.

opts.t: At the concourse, through the LRT entrance, since you're going there anyway
opts.fb: During an alarm the concourse LRT roll shutter closes automatically, so that isn't a way out.

opts.t: At the concourse, then over to the 102 Street pedway
opts.fb: The 102 Street pedway roll shutter also closes automatically during an alarm. Leave at the main floor.

questions.src: ESQ Emergency Procedures 2025 — Alarm Response (Tenants), step 5; Automatic Roll-Shutters

questions.q: You reach the main floor exit door at the bottom of the stairwell. It won't open when you push, and there's a blue pull station beside it. What do you do?

opts.t: Head back up and look for a different stairwell
opts.fb: Going back up puts you against people coming down. This door opens once you release the lock.

opts.t: Use the nearby help station to ask Security to unlock the door
opts.fb: You don't need to wait for Security. The blue pull station releases the door yourself.

opts.t: Pull the blue pull station down to release the lock
opts.fb: It releases the magnetic lock. On doors with a push bar instead, pull up on the bar and push forward.

questions.src: ESQ Emergency Procedures 2025 — Alarm Response (Tenants), step 6

questions.q: You've just left ESQ by the main floor exit during an alarm. Where do you go?

opts.t: Stay on the sidewalk outside the main Jasper Avenue doors
opts.fb: Standing by the doors blocks people coming out and responders going in. Head to the muster point.

opts.t: The upper platform of the Bay/Enterprise Square LRT station
opts.fb: That's ESQ's muster point (use the 103 Street entrance). Wait there for the All Clear.

opts.t: Back down to the concourse level, near the LRT entrance
opts.fb: The concourse is inside the building, and its LRT entrance shutter closes during an alarm. Go to the muster point.

questions.src: ESQ Emergency Procedures 2025 — Alarm Response (Tenants), step 7; ESQ Ready lesson content — Out by the stairs

questions.q: You're at the muster point. The alarm has stopped and the fire trucks are pulling away. Your manager wants everyone back for a 3:00 meeting. When can you go back in?

opts.t: Right away, since the fire department has already left
opts.fb: Building staff still have to reset the alarm system and the elevators. Wait for the All Clear.

opts.t: Once you see the elevators running again from the lobby
opts.fb: Resetting the elevators is only one of the steps. Nobody re-enters until Security gives the All Clear.

opts.t: After the All Clear signal and PA announcement
opts.fb: You'll see a visual All Clear indicator at the muster point and hear a public address (PA) announcement through the building.

questions.src: ESQ Emergency Procedures 2025 — All Clear; Alarm Response (BentallGreenOak)

questions.q: The fire alarm sounds while you're at your desk at ESQ. Which of these do you do before you head for the stairs? Select all that apply.

opts.t: End your call and close your drawers and file cabinets
opts.fb: Correct. It takes seconds and is the first step in the tenant procedure.

opts.t: Pick up your keys, wallet, coat and safe shoes
opts.fb: Correct. You may be outside for a while in Edmonton weather.

opts.t: Save your open files and shut down your computer
opts.fb: Not part of the procedure. Saving work costs time you may need to get out.

opts.t: Wait for the Floor Warden to tell you to leave
opts.fb: An alarm means everyone leaves. Floor Wardens direct people to exits, but you don't wait for permission.

questions.src: ESQ Emergency Procedures 2025 — Alarm Response (Tenants), steps 1–2
questions.fb: End calls, close drawers and cabinets, grab keys, wallet and coat, then take the stairs. (In a violent-person situation, leave everything.)

questions.q: Walking past the copy room, you see smoke and a flame coming from a recycling bin. No one else is in the room. What do you do first?

opts.t: Look for the nearest extinguisher and try to put it out
opts.fb: Personal safety comes first. Use an extinguisher only if you're trained, the fire is small, it's safe and you have a clear way out.

opts.t: Leave the room, warn people nearby, and close the door behind you
opts.fb: A closed door helps hold back fire and smoke. Next, pull the nearest fire alarm and call 911.

opts.t: Stay at the doorway and call 911 so you can describe the fire as it grows
opts.fb: Calling 911 matters, but not from beside the fire. Get out, close the door and pull the alarm first.

questions.src: ESQ Ready lesson content — If you discover a fire

questions.q: You've closed the copy room door on a small fire. There's a pull station on the wall by the stairwell. A colleague says, "Let's call Security and let them decide." What do you do?

opts.t: Call Security first so they can check it out
opts.fb: That delays the alarm while the fire grows. Pulling the alarm gets everyone moving right away.

opts.t: Wait a minute for the smoke detectors to set off the alarm
opts.fb: Don't wait on the detectors. If you've found a fire, pull the alarm yourself.

opts.t: Pull the alarm, then call 911 and evacuate by the stairs
opts.fb: Give 911 the address, 10230 Jasper Avenue, and where the fire is.

questions.src: ESQ Ready lesson content — If you discover a fire

questions.q: You're in the ESQ parkade when the fire alarm sounds. Your car is parked right beside you. What do you do?

opts.t: Drive out quickly before the exits get busy
opts.fb: Never remove a vehicle from the parkade during an alarm. Moving cars put people walking out at risk.

opts.t: Leave the car and evacuate on foot
opts.fb: Cars are the main fire risk in the parkade, and in a confined space their smoke is a serious hazard. Walk out and go to the muster point.

opts.t: Wait in your car with the doors locked until the All Clear
opts.fb: A car is no shelter. Sprinklers may not stop a car fire, and smoke builds up fast in a confined parkade.

questions.src: ESQ Emergency Procedures 2025 — Parkade

questions.q: A wastebasket near you catches fire. It's small, and there's an extinguisher on the wall. You've never been trained to use one. What's the safest choice?

opts.t: Use it. The PASS steps are easy enough to follow
opts.fb: Knowing the steps isn't the same as being trained. Untrained use can put you in danger.

opts.t: Hand it to the nearest colleague and let them try
opts.fb: They may not be trained either. Only a trained person should use an extinguisher, and only when it's safe.

opts.t: Leave, close the door, and pull the alarm
opts.fb: That's the right call when you aren't trained. Never risk your life to put out a fire.

questions.src: ESQ Ready lesson content — If you discover a fire

questions.q: You're trained to use an extinguisher. In PASS (Pull, Aim, Squeeze, Sweep), where do you aim?

opts.t: At the top of the flames, where they're tallest
opts.fb: Aiming high misses the fuel. The flames keep burning from the bottom.

opts.t: At the base of the fire
opts.fb: That's where the fuel is. Sweep side to side, and if the fire grows, leave and close the door.

opts.t: At the smoke, to clear the air so you can see
opts.fb: Smoke isn't the fire. Aim at the base, where the fuel is burning.

questions.src: ESQ Ready lesson content — If you discover a fire (PASS)

questions.q: You should be able to find a fire extinguisher without thinking. Where are ESQ's base-building extinguishers kept?

opts.t: In kitchens, lunchrooms and at the main floor Security desk
opts.fb: There are more than that. Extinguishers are in every main hallway, stairwell and mechanical room.

opts.t: In every main hallway, stairwell and mechanical room
opts.fb: Tenant spaces may also have extra extinguishers of their own, so check where yours are.

opts.t: In each elevator lobby, next to the mobility rescue location
opts.fb: That isn't where they're listed. Check main hallways, emergency stairwells and mechanical rooms.

questions.src: ESQ Emergency Procedures 2025 — Life Safety Systems 2.4; ESQ Ready lesson content — Spot a fire (Learn)

questions.q: During an alarm, a colleague notices the air vents have gone quiet and worries the building has lost power. What's actually happening?

opts.t: The ventilation shuts down to stop smoke spreading, and exhaust fans pull smoke out
opts.fb: The HVAC fans stop so smoke doesn't travel between floors, while emergency exhaust fans remove it from the building.

opts.t: There's a power failure, so you should turn off your equipment and wait
opts.fb: Quiet vents during an alarm are part of the fire response, not a power failure. Keep evacuating.

opts.t: A fault in the ventilation is what set off the alarm
opts.fb: The ventilation shuts down because of the alarm, to keep smoke from spreading.

questions.src: ESQ Emergency Procedures 2025 — Life Safety Systems 2.5

questions.q: On ESQ's emergency floor plans, what does an orange striped bar mark?

opts.t: An area that's closed during an alarm
opts.fb: Closed areas, like the roll shutters, are marked with a red NO EXIT sign instead.

opts.t: An emergency exit door
opts.fb: Red EXIT arrows mark the emergency stairwells themselves.

opts.t: A fire-rated wall or fire door
opts.fb: The plans don't use orange bars for walls. They mark emergency exit doors.

questions.src: ESQ Ready lesson content — Read your floor plan

questions.q: What does the blue wheelchair symbol mark on an ESQ floor plan?

opts.t: The accessible entrance and ramp on the main floor of the building
opts.fb: It appears on every floor, not just the main floor. It marks where people who need help on stairs wait during an alarm.

opts.t: The nearest accessible washroom
opts.fb: It isn't a washroom sign. It marks the mobility rescue location.

opts.t: The mobility rescue location at the elevator lobby
opts.fb: On every floor, that's where people who need help on stairs wait with their two helpers for emergency responders.

questions.src: ESQ Ready lesson content — Read your floor plan; ESQ Emergency Procedures 2025 — Individuals with Mobility Restrictions

questions.q: The concourse floor plan shows a red NO EXIT sign at the LRT entrance. Why?

opts.t: It's kept clear for emergency responders coming in
opts.fb: Responders don't use it either. A roll shutter closes there during an alarm.

opts.t: A roll shutter closes there automatically during an alarm
opts.fb: The same happens at the 102 Street pedway. Use a stairwell and exit at the main floor.

opts.t: The LRT stops running whenever the building alarm sounds
opts.fb: The sign is about the building, not the trains. The shutter closes so no one can enter during an emergency.

questions.src: ESQ Ready lesson content — Read your floor plan; ESQ Emergency Procedures 2025 — Automatic Roll-Shutters

questions.q: On the emergency floor plans, what do the green arrows show?

opts.t: The way to the mobility rescue location
opts.fb: That location is marked with the blue wheelchair symbol at the elevator lobby.

opts.t: The route to the nearest first aid kit
opts.fb: First aid kits aren't shown with green arrows. The arrows mark the muster point.

opts.t: The direction of the muster point
opts.fb: The muster point is the top platform of the Bay/Enterprise Square LRT station.

questions.src: ESQ Ready lesson content — Read your floor plan

questions.title: Your two stairwells
questions.q: You've just moved to the desk marked 'You are here'. Your manager points to the nearest red EXIT arrow and says you're all set. Tap the TWO stairwells you'd use, in case one is blocked.

hotspot.image: ESQ floor plan for your floor with a 'You are here' desk marker. Shows the standard symbols: red EXIT arrows at the emergency stairwells along the outside walls, orange striped bars at exit doors, the blue wheelchair sign at the elevator lobby near the centre of the floor, the red heart (AED) and green muster arrows.

targets.desc: The emergency stairwell (red EXIT arrow) nearest the desk marker, on the outside wall
targets.fb: That's your first way out. Now make sure you know a second one.

targets.desc: A second emergency stairwell (red EXIT arrow) in a different direction from the desk marker, also on an outside wall
targets.fb: Good. Smoke or debris can block a stairwell, so you know a second way out. On every floor the stairwells are along the outside walls.

hotspot.miss_fb: Look along the outside walls for the red EXIT arrows. Those mark the emergency stairwells. The blue wheelchair sign in the middle of the floor is the mobility rescue location at the elevator lobby, not a way out.

list_alternative.t: Find a second stairwell in case the first one is blocked
list_alternative.fb: Smoke or debris can block a stairwell. On every floor the stairwells are along the outside walls.

list_alternative.t: Nothing. All stairwells lead to the same main floor exits
list_alternative.fb: They do all lead down, but one can be blocked by smoke. You need to know a second way out.

list_alternative.t: Nothing. You'll follow the crowd if the alarm sounds
list_alternative.fb: The crowd may head for a blocked route, or you may be alone after hours. Know two stairwells yourself.

questions.src: ESQ Ready lesson content — Read your floor plan; ESQ Emergency Procedures 2025 — Life Safety Systems 2.7
questions.note: Sources say only that stairwells are along the outside walls on every floor; they don't give stairwell positions per floor. Builder: use the real floor plan PDF (linked in the app) and place the desk marker so the two nearest stairwells are clearly in different directions. Accept any two distinct stairwells, or only the two nearest — SME to decide.

questions.title: Find the help station
questions.q: You're at the desk marked 'You are here' on the 3rd floor. Your phone is dead, and a colleague needs ESQ Security urgently. Tap the help station you'd use.

hotspot.image: ESQ 3rd floor plan with a 'You are here' desk marker, showing hallway 3-127 and its stairwell landing, the red fire alarm pull stations, the red EXIT arrows and the elevator lobby (blue wheelchair sign).

targets.desc: The help station on the stairwell landing in hallway 3-127
targets.fb: Right. Help stations connect straight to the ESQ Security desk, for medical emergencies, threats, or when you don't have a phone.

hotspot.miss_fb: Look for the help station on the stairwell landing in hallway 3-127. A red pull station would sound the fire alarm and evacuate the whole building, and waiting in the elevator lobby for a patrol may take too long.

list_alternative.t: Pull the nearest fire alarm so Security comes up to the floor
list_alternative.fb: That evacuates the whole building. A help station connects you to Security directly.

list_alternative.t: Use the help station to reach Security
list_alternative.fb: Help stations connect straight to the ESQ Security desk, for medical emergencies, threats, or when you don't have a phone.

list_alternative.t: Wait by the elevator lobby for a Security patrol to pass by
list_alternative.fb: There's no guarantee a patrol will come by. The help station reaches Security right away.

questions.src: ESQ Emergency Procedures 2025 — Life Safety Systems 2.6; ESQ Ready lesson content — Spot a fire (help stations)
questions.note: Target location comes from the live app's FLOORS data (3rd floor help station: stairwell landing in hallway 3-127). Fixed to the 3rd floor because the app lists help-station locations per floor (concourse: lobby near the LRT entrance; main floor: washroom hallway 1-046; 2nd floor: top of the east and west escalators; 3rd floor: stairwell landing in hallway 3-127; 4th floor: none listed). Confirm help stations actually appear on the posted floor plans; if they don't, the builder must add a marker from the floor data. Don't build a 4th floor version.

questions.q: Which of these colleagues should tell their manager or Floor Warden that they'd need help on the stairs in an alarm? Select all that apply.

opts.t: Dana, who is late in her pregnancy and finds stairs hard
opts.fb: Correct. Pregnancy is named in ESQ's procedures.

opts.t: Raj, who sprained his ankle and is on crutches for three weeks
opts.fb: Correct. Temporary needs count, including sports injuries and broken limbs.

opts.t: Lee, whose heart condition makes several flights of stairs unsafe
opts.fb: Correct. A heart condition is named in ESQ's procedures.

opts.t: Sam, who simply prefers the elevator
opts.fb: Preference isn't the test. The plan is for anyone who needs help getting down the stairs.

questions.src: ESQ Emergency Procedures 2025 — Individuals with Mobility Restrictions
questions.fb: A mobility-restricted person is anyone who needs help down the stairwells, permanently or temporarily. It's up to each person to speak up so a plan is in place.

questions.q: A teammate with a heart condition tells you privately that four flights of stairs would be too much for them. What's the best next step?

opts.t: Tell Security about them yourself, so they're on the list
opts.fb: It's their information to share. Encourage them to tell their manager or Floor Warden, who will plan with them.

opts.t: Encourage them to tell their manager or Floor Warden
opts.fb: It's each person's responsibility to identify themselves. The Floor Warden then assigns two helpers and Security is informed.

opts.t: Tell them to take the elevator if there's ever an alarm
opts.fb: Elevators return to the main floor and stop during an alarm. They aren't an evacuation route.

questions.src: ESQ Emergency Procedures 2025 — Individuals with Mobility Restrictions

questions.q: How many helpers should be assigned to each person who needs help on the stairs?

opts.t: Whoever is closest when the alarm sounds
opts.fb: Help needs to be arranged in advance. Helpers should know their role before any alarm.

opts.t: One, usually the person who sits nearest
opts.fb: One isn't enough. The minimum is two pre-determined helpers.

opts.t: At least two, chosen ahead of time
opts.fb: The Floor Warden assigns two helpers to each person and makes sure a pre-arranged plan is in place.

questions.src: ESQ Emergency Procedures 2025 — Tenants; Floor Wardens; Individuals with Mobility Restrictions

questions.q: The alarm sounds. Your colleague on crutches is at her desk, and her two helpers have just arrived. Where do the three of them go?

opts.t: To the elevator lobby on their floor to wait for responders
opts.fb: That's the mobility designated area on every floor. Emergency responders come there.

opts.t: To the nearest stairwell landing, to wait there out of the crowd
opts.fb: Stairwells are for people evacuating. The designated area is the elevator lobby.

opts.t: Down to the main floor in the elevator before it shuts off
opts.fb: During an alarm, elevators return to the main floor and stop. They aren't used for evacuation.

questions.src: ESQ Emergency Procedures 2025 — Individuals with Mobility Restrictions

questions.q: You're one of two helpers waiting in the elevator lobby with a colleague who can't use the stairs. The Floor Warden has finished checking the floor and left. How long do you stay?

opts.t: Until the floor is empty, then help them down the stairs
opts.fb: People who need help on stairs aren't to self-evacuate. Moving them down a busy stairwell puts you both at risk.

opts.t: About 15 minutes, then call Security to ask what to do
opts.fb: There's no time limit. Stay with them until responders arrive or the All Clear is given.

opts.t: Until emergency responders arrive or Security gives the All Clear
opts.fb: The Floor Warden reports to Security that you're there, so responders know where to find you.

questions.src: ESQ Emergency Procedures 2025 — Individuals with Mobility Restrictions; Floor Wardens

questions.q: At 8:00 PM, your colleague Sam phones you. He's alone on the 4th floor, on crutches, and the fire alarm is sounding. What should he do?

opts.t: Go to the elevator lobby and call 911 with his floor and location
opts.fb: He stays there until he's rescued or Security gives the All Clear.

opts.t: Stay at his desk and wait there until Security does its hourly floor check
opts.fb: Don't wait for a routine check. He should go to the elevator lobby, where responders look, and call 911.

opts.t: Take the stairs slowly, holding the rail, and call you back
opts.fb: People who need help on stairs aren't to go down on their own. The elevator lobby is the safe place to wait.

questions.src: ESQ Emergency Procedures 2025 — Individuals with Mobility Restrictions, After Hours Alarm Response

questions.q: After hours, a colleague who can't use the stairs is waiting in the elevator lobby during an alarm, but their phone is at their desk. How can they reach Security?

opts.t: Pull the fire alarm again so Security knows someone's there
opts.fb: The alarm is already sounding, so pulling it again sends no new information. A help station connects to Security.

opts.t: Use a help station to call Security
opts.fb: Help stations go straight to the Security desk. Then stay in the elevator lobby until rescued or the All Clear.

opts.t: Wait, because Security will see their name in the logbook
opts.fb: Checking in helps responders know someone may be inside, but it doesn't tell them where. Reach Security directly if you can.

questions.src: ESQ Emergency Procedures 2025 — Individuals with Mobility Restrictions, After Hours Alarm Response

questions.q: On a warm afternoon, someone has wedged a stairwell door open to get some airflow on your floor. What do you do?

opts.t: Leave it. The doors unlock during an alarm anyway
opts.fb: The issue isn't locking. Stairwell doors must stay closed because a closed door helps hold back fire and smoke.

opts.t: Remove the wedge and let the door close
opts.fb: Stairwell doors stay closed at all times. If it keeps happening, report it to ClikFix: 1-866-254-5349.

opts.t: Leave it, but tape up a sign asking people to close it later
opts.fb: A sign doesn't protect the stairwell now. Close the door yourself.

questions.src: ESQ Emergency Procedures 2025 — Safety Suggestions, General Hazards

questions.q: You're stacking boxes of workshop supplies on a storage-room shelf just under a sprinkler head. How much space do you leave below and around the sprinkler?

opts.t: 6 inches
opts.fb: That's too little. Sprinklers need room to spray properly.

opts.t: 18 inches
opts.fb: Keep stored items at least 18 inches below and around sprinkler heads so they can spray properly.

opts.t: 36 inches
opts.fb: More than the rule. Keep at least 18 inches below and around sprinkler heads.

questions.src: ESQ Emergency Procedures 2025 — Safety Suggestions, General Hazards; ESQ Ready lesson content — Spot the hazards (Learn)

questions.q: For a team celebration, a colleague wants to hang streamers and a banner from the exposed sprinkler pipes in the meeting room. What do you say?

opts.t: It's fine if the decorations are light paper
opts.fb: Weight isn't the issue. Nothing should hang from sprinkler heads or piping.

opts.t: It's fine as long as it's all taken down again the same afternoon
opts.fb: Even for a few hours, anything hanging from sprinklers can stop them working. Find another anchor.

opts.t: Hang them somewhere else. Nothing goes on sprinkler pipes
opts.fb: Nothing hangs from sprinkler heads or piping, ever. Keep decorations 18 inches clear too.

questions.src: ESQ Emergency Procedures 2025 — Safety Suggestions, General Hazards

questions.q: Your desk is chilly, and a colleague offers you their small electric space heater. What do you do?

opts.t: Use the heater on its lowest setting and switch it off when you leave
opts.fb: ESQ's rule is no space heaters, whatever the setting. They can start fires.

opts.t: Use the heater, but run it just while you're sitting right beside it
opts.fb: Being nearby doesn't remove the fire risk. ESQ's rule is no space heaters.

opts.t: Thank them, but keep the heater out of the office
opts.fb: ESQ's rule is no space heaters. If you need warmth at your desk, the ESQ booklet suggests a "Cozy Leg" style warmer, designed not to cause combustion.

questions.src: ESQ Emergency Procedures 2025 — Safety Suggestions, Electrical Hazards; ESQ Ready lesson content — Spot the hazards (Power, safely)

questions.q: At a hot desk, your laptop cord won't reach the outlet. A colleague suggests running an extension cord under the rug so no one trips. What do you do?

opts.t: Run it under the rug, since that keeps it flat and out of everyone's way
opts.fb: Cords under rugs or mats get damaged without anyone noticing. Extension cords must never run under mats or carpets.

opts.t: Tape it flat across the walkway instead
opts.fb: Cords stretched across walkways get stepped on and damaged. Find a protected route or a closer outlet.

opts.t: Find a route where the cord is protected and not under anything
opts.fb: Extension cords should be protected from physical damage. Replace any cord that's frayed or cracked.

questions.src: ESQ Emergency Procedures 2025 — Safety Suggestions, Electrical Hazards

questions.q: You see a contractor smoking in a stairwell inside ESQ. What do you do?

opts.t: Report it to Security right away
opts.fb: ESQ is a non-smoking building, and careless smoking is a major cause of fires.

opts.t: Report it to ClikFix as an unsafe condition
opts.fb: ClikFix handles repairs and building conditions. Someone smoking onsite goes to Security.

opts.t: Ask them to put it out, and leave it there
opts.fb: They may light up again elsewhere. The booklet asks you to report anyone smoking onsite to Security.

questions.src: ESQ Emergency Procedures 2025 — Safety Suggestions, General Hazards

questions.q: On your floor, a stack of chairs is blocking a fire extinguisher, and the light above a stairwell exit has gone out. What do you do?

opts.t: Tell Security at the front desk on your way out
opts.fb: Security handles threats, medical calls and check-ins. Building problems like exit lights go to ClikFix.

opts.t: Move the chairs if you can, and report the light to ClikFix
opts.fb: Keep the space around extinguishers, pull stations and stairwell doors clear. ClikFix: 1-866-254-5349.

opts.t: Email your manager to raise both at the next team meeting
opts.fb: Unsafe conditions should be fixed now, not next week. Clear what you can and report the rest to ClikFix.

questions.src: ESQ Emergency Procedures 2025 — Tenants; Floor Wardens Day to Day

questions.q: You're helping tidy a storage room at ESQ. Which of these are fire hazards to fix or report? Select all that apply.

opts.t: Boxes stacked a few inches below a sprinkler head
opts.fb: Correct. Stored items need 18 inches of clearance below and around sprinklers.

opts.t: Large piles of old paper and empty boxes
opts.fb: Correct. Paper and boxes are fuel for a fire. Don't let them pile up.

opts.t: A power bar with no circuit protection
opts.fb: Correct. Power bars need circuit protection.

opts.t: An extension cord running under a floor mat
opts.fb: Correct. Cords under rugs or mats get damaged without anyone noticing.

opts.t: A stairwell door that's closed
opts.fb: That's exactly how it should be. Stairwell doors stay closed to hold back fire and smoke.

questions.src: ESQ Emergency Procedures 2025 — Safety Suggestions; ESQ Ready lesson content — Spot the hazards (Learn)
questions.fb: Fewer piles, clear sprinklers and protected power keep small problems from becoming fires. Report what you can't fix to ClikFix.

questions.q: What's the number for the ESQ Security desk, staffed 24/7?

opts.fb: That's the Edmonton Police Service non-emergency line.
That's the BentallGreenOak management office.
Save it in your phone. It's the number for check-ins, the safety phrase and any security concern.

questions.src: ESQ Emergency Procedures 2025 — Important Telephone Numbers

questions.q: A visitor in your suite is getting agitated and watching you closely. You want Security without tipping them off. Which call gets the right response?

opts.t: "Can you bring me a coffee? I'm in 2-334."
opts.fb: Phrase first, then your suite. Security sends an officer right away and puts other staff on standby.

opts.t: "Hi, I'm in 2-334. Can you bring me a coffee?"
opts.fb: Close, but the order matters. Say the phrase first so Security knows to record the location that follows.

opts.t: "Hi, it's me. Could someone come up when they have a minute?"
opts.fb: That sounds routine, and Security has no location. Use the phrase, then your suite number.

questions.src: ESQ Emergency Procedures 2025 — Security Safety Phrase

questions.q: You've called Security and said, "Can you bring me a coffee?" You can't safely say much more. What's the minimum you need to add?

opts.t: Your name and your department
opts.fb: Helpful in other calls, but it won't get an officer to you. Your suite number is the essential detail.

opts.t: Your suite number
opts.fb: Add details like where you are in the space only if you can do it without raising suspicion.

opts.t: A description of the person
opts.fb: Describing them out loud could escalate things. Give your suite number; officers come to you.

questions.src: ESQ Emergency Procedures 2025 — Security Safety Phrase

questions.q: In a shared hallway at ESQ, a man is shouting threats at your coworker and stepping closer. What should you do?

opts.t: Step between them and try to calm him down
opts.fb: Don't confront a violent person. Your priority is to get yourself away from the situation.

opts.t: Stay back where it's safer and record it on your phone as evidence
opts.fb: Staying puts you at risk. Leave first; you can report details afterward.

opts.t: Get away, warn others, then call 911 and ESQ Security
opts.fb: Remain calm and leave. Tell others to leave too if they can do so safely.

questions.src: ESQ Emergency Procedures 2025 — Violent Persons Procedures

questions.q: At ESQ, you've escaped into a meeting room from a person who threatened violence. They're still out in the hallway. What now?

opts.t: Lock and block the door, then call 911 and ESQ Security
opts.fb: Put distance and barriers between you and the person. Report it as soon as you can.

opts.t: Open the door a little to see where they've gone
opts.fb: That removes your barrier. Stay locked in and call for help.

opts.t: Leave by the hallway to go and find a Security officer
opts.fb: The person is in the hallway. Stay behind the locked, blocked door and call.

questions.src: ESQ Emergency Procedures 2025 — Violent Persons Procedures

questions.q: You hear what sounds like gunfire on your floor. The nearest stairwell is clear and away from the sound. Your laptop and bag are at your desk. What do you do?

opts.t: Grab your laptop and bag first, then leave by the clear stairwell
opts.fb: This isn't a fire alarm. Leave your belongings behind; every second counts.

opts.t: Leave now, warning others but not waiting for them
opts.fb: Get out if it's safe, leaving your belongings. Once you're somewhere safe, call 911.

opts.t: Stay at your desk until you know what's going on
opts.fb: Waiting to be sure costs time. If you can get out safely, go now.

questions.src: ESQ Emergency Procedures 2025 — Active Shooter Procedures

questions.q: You suspect gunfire nearby and can't get out safely. You're in an office with a door that locks. What do you do?

opts.t: Hide, and leave your phone's ringer on so responders can find you
opts.fb: A ringing phone could give away your hiding place. Silence your devices.

opts.t: Lock and block the door, turn off the lights, and silence your phone
opts.fb: Stay silent and still. If you can, contact 911 silently by text or with a sign in the window.

opts.t: Call 911 and describe out loud what you're hearing
opts.fb: Talking out loud could reveal where you are. Communicate silently if you can.

questions.src: ESQ Emergency Procedures 2025 — Active Shooter Procedures

questions.q: At ESQ, a colleague collapses in the staff lunchroom and isn't responding. Who do you call first?

opts.t: ESQ Security, so they can bring the AED
opts.fb: Security matters, but they come second. Call 911 first so the ambulance is on its way.

opts.t: 911, to request an ambulance
opts.fb: Then call ESQ Security at 780-428-1541 and tell them an ambulance is coming.

opts.t: Health Link at 811, to ask what to do
opts.fb: Health Link is for non-emergency health advice. Someone who has collapsed needs 911.

questions.src: ESQ Emergency Procedures 2025 — Medical Emergency Procedures

questions.q: At ESQ, you're on the phone with the 911 dispatcher about a medical emergency. What should you give them? Select all that apply.

opts.t: The address: 10230 Jasper Avenue, between 102 and 103 Streets
opts.fb: Correct. The cross streets help the ambulance find the building fast.

opts.t: Your name and phone number
opts.fb: Correct. The dispatcher may need to reach you.

opts.t: Your unit and the exact location of the emergency
opts.fb: Correct. This gets responders to the right floor and room.

opts.t: The location of the nearest first aid kit
opts.fb: Not needed by the dispatcher. Security brings first aid and an AED once you call them.

questions.src: ESQ Emergency Procedures 2025 — Medical Emergency Procedures; ESQ Ready lesson content — First on scene (Learn)
questions.fb: Give the dispatcher what gets the ambulance to you: the address, who you are, how to reach you, and exactly where the person is. Stay on the line until the dispatcher hangs up.

questions.q: At ESQ, you've called 911 for a colleague who fainted. Now you call ESQ Security. What do you tell them?

opts.t: Ask them to call 911 too, to make sure your call went through
opts.fb: One 911 call is enough. Tell Security an ambulance is coming so they can get ready.

opts.t: That an ambulance is coming, and exactly where you are
opts.fb: Security then brings first aid and an AED, holds an elevator, and meets paramedics at the street.

opts.t: Ask whether it's okay for paramedics to come up to your floor
opts.fb: No approval is needed. Security guides paramedics to you.

questions.src: ESQ Emergency Procedures 2025 — Medical Emergency Procedures; ESQ Ready lesson content — First on scene

questions.q: At ESQ, a visitor collapses near the main entrance. A colleague is already on the phone with 911. How do you get an AED there fastest?

opts.t: Call ESQ Security at 780-428-1541. They bring first aid and an AED
opts.fb: Security officers are trained in first aid, CPR and AED use, and there's an AED at the main floor Security desk.

opts.t: Search the first aid kits on the main floor for an AED unit
opts.fb: A first aid kit isn't an AED. Call Security: they bring the AED and trained officers.

opts.t: Wait for the paramedics to arrive, since they carry their own AED
opts.fb: Every minute counts. Call Security now: they bring an AED and hold an elevator for paramedics.

questions.src: ESQ Emergency Procedures 2025 — Medical Emergency Procedures; ESQ Ready lesson content — First on scene (Then call Security)

questions.q: At ESQ, a jug of cleaning concentrate splits open in the mail room, and two people nearby feel lightheaded. What do you do?

opts.t: Call Security first so their staff can clean it up
opts.fb: Security is the second call. For a hazardous spill or exposure, dial 911 first.

opts.t: Open a window and wipe it up with paper towels
opts.fb: Don't handle the spill. Keep people away from it and call 911.

opts.t: Call 911, keep people away, then call Security
opts.fb: Give 911 the address and location in the building, then tell Security what's happening and follow responders' instructions.

questions.src: ESQ Emergency Procedures 2025 — Hazardous Materials Procedures

questions.q: You're calling the ESQ Security desk to check in for an evening of work. What should you give them? Select all that apply.

opts.t: Your name, exact location and phone number
opts.fb: Correct. Security needs to know who you are, where to find you and how to reach you.

opts.t: When you expect to leave
opts.fb: Correct. Call back if it changes.

opts.t: Your building access card number
opts.fb: Not part of the check-in. Give your name, location, phone and when you'll leave.

opts.t: Your manager's home phone number
opts.fb: Not needed. Working alone? Tell your supervisor too, but you don't give Security their home number.

questions.src: ESQ Emergency Procedures 2025 — Working After Hours; ESQ Ready lesson content — Working late
questions.fb: Security uses check-ins to make sure everyone is out safely in an emergency, and checks on you hourly.

questions.q: On Saturday morning you pop into ESQ to finish some slides. You'll only be there two hours, and no one else from your team is in. What do you need to do?

opts.t: Nothing, since it's a short visit
opts.fb: Any after-hours or weekend work counts, however short. Security needs to know you're in the building.

opts.t: Just let Security know when you leave
opts.fb: Checking in at the start is what matters, so Security knows you're inside if something happens.

opts.t: Tell your supervisor and check in
opts.fb: Sign the After Hours Logbook, email esqsecurity@bgo.com, or call 780-428-1541.

questions.src: ESQ Emergency Procedures 2025 — Working After Hours

questions.q: You checked in with Security at 6:00 PM, saying you'd leave at 8:00. It's 8:00 now and you need another hour. What do you do?

opts.t: Call Security to update your departure time
opts.fb: Contact Security whenever your plans change so their records match where you are.

opts.t: Nothing. Security checks on you every hour anyway
opts.fb: Hourly checks don't replace an update. Let Security know your new departure time.

opts.t: Sign the logbook again on your way out
opts.fb: That's too late to help if something happens before you leave. Call now with the change.

questions.src: ESQ Emergency Procedures 2025 — Working After Hours

questions.q: It's 8:40 PM. The fire alarm sounds, and you get out to the muster point. You're cold and want to head straight home. What should you do first?

opts.t: Head home. Security can see your name in the logbook
opts.fb: That's the problem: if you signed in but don't report out, responders will assume you're still inside.

opts.t: Tell Security that you're out of the building
opts.fb: Otherwise emergency responders may search the building for you.

opts.t: Text your supervisor that you made it out safely
opts.fb: Your supervisor isn't directing the search. Report to Security so they know you're out.

questions.src: ESQ Emergency Procedures 2025 — Individuals with Mobility Restrictions, After Hours; Working After Hours

questions.q: It's 9:30 PM and dark. Your car is a block away from ESQ and you'd rather not walk alone. What's your best option?

opts.t: Call the Students' Union Safewalk
opts.fb: That's a different service. ESQ's Safe Walk is run by Paladin Security and booked through ESQ Security.

opts.t: Ask ESQ Security for a Safe Walk
opts.fb: It's free within two blocks of ESQ. Call 780-428-1541 or visit the desk, ideally about an hour ahead.

opts.t: Call the police non-emergency line for an escort
opts.fb: Police don't provide this service. ESQ Security offers a Safe Walk within two blocks.

questions.src: ESQ Ready lesson content — Working late (Safe Walk)

questions.q: At 7:00 PM, you notice someone you don't recognize loitering by your suite's locked door. What do you do?

opts.t: Ask whether they need help finding someone
opts.fb: Approaching them could put you at risk. Keep your distance and let Security check.

opts.t: Let them in if they say they forgot their access card
opts.fb: You can't confirm who they are. Don't let them in; call Security instead.

opts.t: Keep your distance and call Security at 780-428-1541
opts.fb: Loitering near locked doors is a listed warning sign. Security can check safely.

questions.src: ESQ Emergency Procedures 2025 — Suspicious Behavior and Individuals

questions.q: After hours, a man walks into your suite. He's polite, but something about him makes you uneasy. What do you do?

opts.t: Call building Security at 780-428-1541
opts.fb: You don't need proof of a threat. If you feel uncomfortable after someone enters your workplace, call Security.

opts.t: Wait and see whether he does anything suspicious
opts.fb: Feeling uncomfortable is reason enough. Calling early gives Security time to respond.

opts.t: Ask him to show you his ID before you call anyone
opts.fb: Challenging him could escalate things. Call Security and let them handle it.

questions.src: ESQ Emergency Procedures 2025 — Working After Hours

questions.q: You'll be working alone in your suite until 9 PM tonight. Which plan-ahead step fits ESQ's guidance?

opts.t: Leave your suite door unlocked so Security can check on you
opts.fb: The guidance is the opposite: close and lock doors after normal hours.

opts.t: Carry a cell phone, and close and lock doors after hours
opts.fb: Also check in with Security, tell your supervisor, and know your exits.

opts.t: Prop the stairwell door open so you can get out faster later
opts.fb: Stairwell doors stay closed at all times. Plan your exit route instead.

questions.src: ESQ Emergency Procedures 2025 — Working After Hours, Plan Ahead; ESQ Ready lesson content — Working late (Learn)

questions.q: At 10:00 AM the power fails across your floor and the emergency lights come on. What do you do?

opts.t: Turn off your electrical equipment and wait for building management
opts.fb: That lowers the load on circuits when power returns. Management will tell you the cause and what to do next.

opts.t: Evacuate by the stairs right away
opts.fb: A power failure on its own isn't an evacuation. If you need to leave, building management will tell you, or the alarm will sound.

opts.t: Leave everything switched on so you'll know when power is back
opts.fb: Equipment left on adds load to the circuits when power returns. Turn it off.

questions.src: ESQ Emergency Procedures 2025 — Power Failure Procedures

questions.q: From your window, you see what looks like a funnel cloud forming south of downtown. What do you do?

opts.t: Post a photo in the team chat and keep a close eye on how it develops
opts.fb: That doesn't alert the people who can act. Report suspected weather emergencies to building Security.

opts.t: Report it to building Security and follow building staff
opts.fb: Security and building personnel coordinate the response, including any move within the building.

opts.t: Go home now, before it reaches downtown
opts.fb: Heading out into severe weather can be more dangerous. Report it and follow building staff.

questions.src: ESQ Emergency Procedures 2025 — Weather-Related Emergency Procedures

questions.q: A severe storm is approaching downtown. Which of these are part of ESQ's weather procedure? Select all that apply.

opts.t: Power down your electrical equipment
opts.fb: Correct. It's the first step in the procedure.

opts.t: Move critical belongings away from windows
opts.fb: Correct. Secure them in an enclosed room if you can.

opts.t: Have a flashlight and, if available, an AM/FM radio for local news
opts.fb: Correct. Tenants are encouraged to keep flashlights handy.

opts.t: Take the elevator down to a lower floor
opts.fb: If you need to leave your area, use the stairwells, not the elevators.

opts.t: Open the windows slightly to balance the air pressure
opts.fb: That isn't in the procedure. Stay a safe distance from windows.

questions.src: ESQ Emergency Procedures 2025 — Weather-Related Emergency Procedures
questions.fb: Power down, move valuables away from windows, keep a light and radio handy, and follow building staff.

questions.q: High winds are battering the building and the window beside you looks like it may break. What do you do?

opts.t: Tape an X across the glass and stay at your desk
opts.fb: Tape won't protect you from breaking glass. Get away from the window.

opts.t: Go to the elevator lobby and take the elevator down
opts.fb: Use stairwells, not elevators, if you need to move during a storm.

opts.t: Take cover in a stairwell or under sturdy furniture
opts.fb: Protect your head and neck, stay away from exterior walls and hold on. Afterward, tell building staff about any damage or injuries.

questions.src: ESQ Emergency Procedures 2025 — Weather-Related Emergency Procedures

questions.q: Freezing rain has made the roads dangerous by the end of the workday. What does ESQ's procedure suggest?

opts.t: Arrange a local hotel, or be ready to stay in the building
opts.fb: Staying in the building is at building management's discretion. Keep calls to family short.

opts.t: Leave right away, before the roads get any worse
opts.fb: If travel is dangerous, staying put is safer than driving in it.

opts.t: Wait it out in your car in the parkade
opts.fb: That isn't part of the procedure. Arrange a hotel or stay in the building if management allows.

questions.src: ESQ Emergency Procedures 2025 — Weather-Related Emergency Procedures

questions.q: Water is dripping from the ceiling onto a power bar in a meeting room. What do you do?

opts.t: Put a bin under the drip and email facilities about it later in the day
opts.fb: A leak near electrical equipment needs a quick response. Call ClikFix now.

opts.t: Call ClikFix, and power down nearby equipment if it's safe
opts.fb: ClikFix: 1-866-254-5349. Move belongings away from the water and follow building staff.

opts.t: Call 911 to report the leak near the electrical equipment
opts.fb: A leak isn't a 911 emergency on its own. ClikFix handles floods and urgent repairs.

questions.src: ESQ Ready lesson content — Power, storms & floods (Flooding)

questions.q: The U of A tells everyone at ESQ to shelter in place because of a hazardous release nearby. What should you do? Select all that apply.

opts.t: Stay inside the building
opts.fb: Correct. Shelter in place means a safe indoor location.

opts.t: Keep doors and windows closed
opts.fb: Correct. This helps keep outside air out.

opts.t: Use your phone only when necessary
opts.fb: Correct. This keeps cellular networks free for emergency responders.

opts.t: Watch university social media and the website for updates

opts.t: Head to the muster point at the LRT station

questions.src: ESQ Emergency Procedures 2025 — Shelter In Place
questions.fb: You may be told to shelter in place during a large chemical release, to avoid violent crime, or when evacuating isn't safe.

questions.q: A caller tells you there's a bomb in the building. Which of these should you do during the call? Select all that apply.

opts.t: Stay calm and keep the caller talking
opts.fb: Correct. The longer they talk, the more you can learn.

opts.t: Ask when it will go off and where it is
opts.fb: Correct. These are on ESQ's bomb threat checklist.

opts.t: Note their voice, accent and any background noise
opts.fb: Correct. These details can help police.

opts.t: Hang up as soon as they stop, so you can call 911
opts.fb: Don't hang up, even after the caller does. Use another phone to call 911, then Security.

questions.src: ESQ Emergency Procedures 2025 — Bomb Threat Procedures; ESQ Ready lesson content — Calls & packages
questions.fb: Listen, don't interrupt, keep them talking, and write everything down. Leave the line open.

questions.q: The bomb threat caller hangs up. What do you do with your phone?

opts.t: Leave the line open, and call 911 from another phone
opts.fb: Don't hang up or disconnect your phone. Then call Security at 780-428-1541, also from another line.

opts.t: Hang up and call 911 from the same phone
opts.fb: Don't disconnect your phone, even after the caller hangs up. Use a different line.

opts.t: Hang up, then dial back the last number to identify the caller
opts.fb: Keep your line connected. Call 911 from another phone and let the police follow up.

questions.src: ESQ Emergency Procedures 2025 — Bomb Threat Procedures

questions.q: You've reported a bomb threat to 911 and Security. Coworkers ask what's going on. What do you do?

opts.t: Tell everyone nearby to start evacuating
opts.fb: Police, Security and management decide what happens next. Don't cause panic by alarming others.

opts.t: Return to your desk and wait for instructions
opts.fb: Stay calm. Responders come to your area right away, and if people need to move, building staff will direct them.

opts.t: Pull the fire alarm so the building empties fast
opts.fb: That could send people past the threat. Let police and Security decide the response.

questions.src: ESQ Emergency Procedures 2025 — Bomb Threat Procedures

questions.q: After a bomb threat call, besides 911 and ESQ Security, who should you contact?

opts.t: Your immediate supervisor
opts.fb: Then wait at your desk for instructions.

opts.t: Your whole team, by email

opts.t: The BentallGreenOak Building Manager
opts.fb: Security brings in building management. Your own call is to your supervisor.

questions.src: ESQ Emergency Procedures 2025 — Bomb Threat Procedures

questions.src: ESQ Emergency Procedures 2025 — Suspicious Package Procedures

questions.q: You've told Security about a suspicious box in the hallway. What's your next step?

opts.t: Move it into an empty room so no one bumps into it

opts.t: Leave it alone and call police at 780-423-4567

opts.t: Open the flaps just enough to look for a name

questions.src: ESQ Emergency Procedures 2025 — Suspicious Package Procedures

questions.q: Over the past week, someone has called your desk phone three times making threats about your team. What do you do?

opts.t: Let it go to voicemail and hope it stops

opts.t: Notify building Security at 780-428-1541 right away
opts.fb: Report any harassing or threatening calls immediately. Security can act on it.

opts.t: Wait for a fourth call before reporting it
opts.fb: Don't wait. Notify Security immediately about any harassing or threatening call.

questions.src: ESQ Emergency Procedures 2025 — Working After Hours, Preventive Workplace Actions

opts.t: Leave the building and go home for the day

opts.fb: This is a relocation within the building, not a fire evacuation. Follow building personnel.

questions.src: ESQ Emergency Procedures 2025 — Important Telephone Numbers; ESQ Ready lesson content — Downtown smarts

questions.q: On the 103 Street sidewalk outside ESQ, someone is lying unconscious and won't respond. What do you do?

questions.src: ESQ Ready lesson content — Downtown smarts

questions.q: A new colleague says workplace safety is really HSE's job, not theirs. What's the best reply?

opts.t: Safe behaviour is each person's responsibility, including ours

opts.t: Mostly true: supervisors and HSE carry the real safety duties
opts.fb: Supervisors and HSE have duties, but safe behaviour is everyone's shared responsibility.

opts.t: True for labs and shops, but much less so for office teams like ours
opts.fb: The commitment covers all faculty, staff, students, contractors and visitors, including office teams.

questions.src: Working Safely (U of A HSE) — University Safety Commitment

questions.title: What do you say?
questions.q: A coworker tells you she avoids mentioning her faith at work because she worries how people will react. What do you say?

opts.t: "I'm glad you told me. You're welcome here as you are, and if something ever feels off, I'll support you."
opts.fb: Right. Cultural safety means no one should have to mask who they are. If she wants to raise a concern, support her.

opts.t: "Faith's a personal thing, so it's probably best kept out of work anyway."
opts.fb: The Culture of Care includes cultural safety, so identity and belonging are part of a safe workplace.

opts.t: "Maybe keep it private for now. Less chance of friction that way."
opts.fb: That asks her to keep masking who she is. Cultural safety means she shouldn't have to.

questions.src: A Culture of Care — Safety definitions (cultural safety)

questions.q: Your colleague is about to step onto the wheeled chair to reach the box on top of the tall cabinet. What do you do?

opts.t: Stop them and point out the danger right away
opts.fb: Right. We stop unsafe work, alert anyone in danger and act quickly to remedy hazards. Then help find a safer way to reach the box.

opts.t: Let it go, since it's their own choice to take the risk
opts.fb: Safe behaviour is a shared responsibility. The commitment asks you to step in, not stay silent.

opts.t: Hold the chair steady for them so they can finish quickly
opts.fb: A steadied wheeled chair is still a wheeled chair. Stop the unsafe work and find a safer way.

questions.src: Working Safely (U of A HSE) — Our Shared Commitment

questions.q: A teammate tells you a cable running across the walkway looks like a trip hazard. Which response reflects Our Shared Commitment?

opts.t: Listen, take it seriously and act on it together.
opts.fb: Right. The commitment says we listen to others' safety concerns and respond respectfully, with a call to action.

opts.t: Thank them, then wait to see if anyone actually trips.
opts.fb: Waiting for an injury ignores the concern. The commitment asks for a respectful response and a call to action.

opts.t: Reassure them the area was looked at recently, so it's fine.
opts.fb: A past check doesn't remove a hazard that's there now. Listen and respond with action.

questions.src: Working Safely (U of A HSE) — Our Shared Commitment

questions.q: Which of these are part of the U of A's shared safety commitment? Select all that apply.

opts.t: We plan our work so it can be done safely.
opts.fb: Yes. Planning the work comes first.

opts.t: We make sure we have the training, skills and tools to work safely.
opts.fb: Yes. This is one of the listed commitments.

opts.t: We support workplaces free of harassment, bullying and intimidation.
opts.fb: Yes. Psychologically safe environments are part of the commitment.

opts.t: We listen to others' safety concerns and respond with a call to action.
opts.fb: Yes. Concerns get a respectful response and action.

opts.t: We leave fixing hazards to supervisors so everyone else can stay focused.
opts.fb: No. The commitment asks everyone to stop unsafe work and act quickly to remedy hazards.

questions.src: Working Safely (U of A HSE) — Our Shared Commitment
questions.fb: The commitment covers planning, training and tools, psychological safety, stopping unsafe work and listening to concerns. Above all, safe behaviour is everyone's responsibility.

questions.q: You don't supervise anyone but want to help your team work safely. Can you be a Safety Champion?

opts.t: Yes. Anyone can be one by keeping themselves and others safe.
opts.fb: Right. The Culture of Care page says anyone can be a Safety Champion, and offers resources for building safety into your day.

opts.t: Not until you've completed the supervisor safety training.

opts.t: Not unless you're a member of a health and safety committee.

questions.src: A Culture of Care — Resources for Safety Champions

questions.q: You're setting up a workshop room tomorrow, and the flip-chart stands are stored on a high shelf. What fits "plan your work so it can be done safely"?

opts.fb: Right. Planning ahead includes making sure you have the training, skills and tools to do the job safely.

opts.t: Climb the shelving carefully when you get there tomorrow
opts.fb: Shelving isn't a ladder. Plan the task and get the right tools first.

opts.t: Decide on the spot tomorrow, since every room is set up differently

questions.src: Working Safely (U of A HSE) — Our Shared Commitment

questions.q: Your manager is away for two weeks and has asked Malik, a senior team member, to act for her. You notice a broken chair in the meeting room. Who do you report it to?

opts.fb: Right. Someone assigned to act for a supervisor during an absence is a supervisor. Ask, "Who is in charge today?"

opts.t: Your manager, by email, once she's back in two weeks
opts.fb: Waiting two weeks leaves the hazard in place. Whoever is in charge today is your supervisor.

opts.t: No one yet, since Malik's job title doesn't include supervisor
opts.fb: Job titles don't decide it. Having charge of a worksite or directing workers is enough.

opts.fb: Right. The first step is to work with your supervisor. A formal work refusal is a last resort.

opts.t: Refuse, and call the Control Centre before saying anything to Malik
opts.fb: You call the Control Centre after you've tried to resolve it with your supervisor and confirmed you're refusing.

opts.t: Do it quickly while a coworker holds the shelving unit steady
opts.fb: If you believe it poses a serious and immediate threat, don't do it. Raise it with your supervisor first.

opts.fb: Right. HSE helps you through the work refusal process.

opts.t: Email hse.info@ualberta.ca, then do the task while you wait for a reply
opts.fb: An official refusal involves a serious and immediate threat. Don't do the work; call the Control Centre now.

opts.t: Wait for the next health and safety committee meeting to raise it formally
opts.fb: A refusal is about a serious and immediate threat, so contact HSE now rather than waiting for a meeting.

questions.src: Working Safely (U of A HSE) — Three worker rights (dangerous work)

opts.fb: Correct. Your regular rate of pay continues.

opts.t: You can't be disciplined, or threatened with discipline, for refusing
opts.fb: Correct. You're protected from discipline for a work refusal.

opts.t: Your pay is put on hold until the investigation ends
opts.fb: No. Your regular rate of pay continues during the investigation.

opts.t: You can be disciplined if the refusal slows the team's work down
opts.fb: No. Disciplinary action, or the threat of it, can't be taken against you for a work refusal.

questions.src: Working Safely (U of A HSE) — Work refusals
questions.fb: During a work refusal you keep your pay and can't be disciplined. If the danger isn't fixed right away, your supervisor investigates and gives you a report.

questions.q: After a work refusal, you think your supervisor hasn't corrected the dangerous work. What should you do?

opts.t: Contact HSE for help at hse.info@ualberta.ca.
opts.fb: Right. Working Safely says to contact HSE if you think the dangerous work hasn't been corrected.

opts.t: Go back to the work, since the report is done.
opts.fb: A finished report doesn't mean the danger is gone. If it isn't corrected, contact HSE.

opts.t: Contact WCB to open a claim about the hazard.
opts.fb: WCB handles reported injuries and illnesses. An uncorrected hazard goes to HSE.

questions.src: Working Safely (U of A HSE) — Work refusals

questions.q: Which of these are among your responsibilities as a worker at the U of A? Select all that apply.

opts.t: Report unsafe behaviours or conditions to your supervisor.
opts.fb: Yes. Report unsafe behaviour or conditions to your supervisor.

opts.t: Avoid causing or taking part in harassment or violent behaviour.
opts.fb: Yes. This is one of your worker responsibilities.

opts.t: Use the devices and PPE your supervisor or employer requires.
opts.fb: Yes. Workers must use required devices and personal protective equipment.

opts.t: Investigate serious incidents yourself before telling anyone.
opts.fb: No. Report to your supervisor. Supervisors and HSE handle investigations.

opts.t: Fix any hazard you find, even if you're not trained to.

questions.src: Working Safely (U of A HSE) — Worker responsibilities
questions.fb: Your responsibilities include taking reasonable care, using required devices and PPE, avoiding harassment and violence, reporting unsafe conditions, and working under a competent worker when a task is new.

questions.q: Your unit is planning a workplace inspection and asks who wants to join. You're not a supervisor. What applies?

opts.fb: Right. The right to participate includes inspections, hazard identification and reviewing safety documents.

opts.t: Inspections are for supervisors and management to carry out.
opts.fb: Supervisors do informal inspections, but workers have the right to take part in workplace inspections.

opts.t: You can comment, but just once the final report has been shared.
opts.fb: Workers can take part in the inspection itself, not just review the result.

questions.src: Working Safely (U of A HSE) — Three worker rights (participation)

questions.q: You're asked to set up the large laminator in the workroom for the first time. Nobody has shown you how, and it gets very hot. What do you do?

opts.t: Ask to be shown the safe procedure, or work beside someone who knows it
opts.fb: Right. You have the right to know safe work procedures, and a new task should be done under a competent worker until you know how.

opts.t: Skim the quick-start page in the manual and get going on your own
opts.fb: A quick skim isn't the same as knowing the safe procedure. Ask, or work alongside someone competent.

opts.t: Formally refuse it as dangerous work and call the Control Centre
opts.fb: A refusal is for a serious and immediate threat. An unfamiliar task first calls for training or a competent worker.

questions.q: You've spotted the cord running across the walkway to the printer. The hazard is identified. What's the next step?

opts.t: Assess the risk: how likely it is to trip someone, and how badly
opts.fb: Right. Identify, assess risk, control, then reassess. It's already caught two people, so the likelihood is high.

opts.t: Report it to your supervisor, then consider the matter closed
opts.fb: Reporting helps, but the cycle doesn't end there. Assess the risk, control it, then reassess.

opts.t: Tape it down and move on, since a cord is a minor trip hazard
opts.fb: Jumping to a quick fix skips assessing the risk, and the cycle ends with checking the control worked.

questions.src: Working Safely (U of A HSE) — Hazard management cycle

questions.q: You assess a hazard and decide it's very likely to hurt someone, and the harm would be serious. What is the risk level?

opts.t: High risk
opts.fb: Right. Risk combines likelihood and consequence: high likelihood × high consequence = high risk.

opts.t: Medium risk, because the two ratings balance out
opts.fb: Likelihood and consequence don't cancel each other. Both being high means high risk.

opts.t: Low risk, as long as no one has been hurt yet
opts.fb: Risk is about the chance and severity of harm, not whether harm has already happened.

questions.src: Working Safely (U of A HSE) — Assessment of risk

questions.q: After a near miss with a low new light fixture, your team posts a sign that says "Watch your head." What type of control is this?

opts.t: Administrative control
opts.fb: Right. Administrative controls change the way people work, using training, signage and safe work practices.

opts.t: Engineering control
opts.fb: Engineering controls isolate people from the hazard, such as a guard or handrail. A sign doesn't do that.

opts.t: Elimination
opts.fb: Elimination physically removes the hazard. The light is still there; the sign only warns people.

questions.src: Working Safely (U of A HSE) — Hierarchy of controls

questions.q: Your team decides to stop storing boxes on top of tall cabinets, so no one has to reach up there at all. What type of control is this?

opts.t: Elimination
opts.fb: Right. Elimination means physically removing the hazard or no longer performing the task.

opts.t: Substitution
opts.fb: Substitution replaces the hazard with something less hazardous. Here the task is removed entirely.

opts.t: Administrative control
opts.fb: Administrative controls change how a task is done. Here the task no longer happens.

questions.src: Working Safely (U of A HSE) — Hierarchy of controls

questions.q: You've put controls in place for a hazard in your workspace. What should happen next?

opts.t: Reassess the hazard to see if the risk is now acceptable.
opts.fb: Right. Reassessment checks whether the controls reduced the risk to an appropriate level.

opts.t: Close the hazard assessment, since controls are now in place.
opts.fb: Controls don't always work as planned. The cycle ends with reassessment, not closure.

opts.t: Wait to see whether any incidents happen over the next month.
opts.fb: Waiting for incidents isn't an assessment. Reassess the hazard with the controls in place.

questions.src: Working Safely (U of A HSE) — Hazard management cycle

questions.q: You notice the cord on your team's shared kettle is frayed. Based on the maintenance guidance, what should happen?

opts.fb: Right. Maintenance includes inspecting equipment and taking defective equipment out of service. Report the unsafe condition to your supervisor.

opts.t: Keep using it carefully until a replacement kettle is bought.
opts.fb: Defective equipment should be taken out of service, not used with extra care.

opts.t: Wrap the cord with tape and keep using it as usual.
opts.fb: Servicing should be done by qualified personnel. A taped cord is still defective equipment.

questions.src: Working Safely (U of A HSE) — Maintenance

questions.title: Fix the cord across the walkway

opts.t: No. Nobody was hurt, so there's nothing for anyone to report
opts.fb: Near misses are reported even when no one is hurt. They help prevent the next, worse incident.

opts.t: Not yet. Wait to see whether it happens to someone else as well
opts.fb: One near miss is enough to report. Waiting risks someone actually getting hurt.

opts.t: Tell your supervisor and find another way with your coworkers.
opts.fb: Right. A broken ladder is unstable. Report it and work with your supervisor and coworkers on another way to get the job done.

opts.t: Use the ladder carefully and just skip the loose step.
opts.fb: A broken ladder is unstable no matter which step you use. You risk injuring yourself and others.

opts.t: Tighten the loose step yourself with a screwdriver, then carry on with the job.
opts.fb: Report the broken ladder to your supervisor. Repairs are done by qualified personnel.

questions.q: You trip over a box in the hallway. You're not hurt and nothing is damaged. What should you do?

opts.t: Report the incident once things are stable, even without injury.
opts.fb: Right. Working Safely says to report the incident even if there appears to be no injury or damage.

opts.t: Move on, since reports are for injuries or damage.
opts.fb: Incidents include near misses. Reporting even minor events helps prevent similar incidents.

opts.t: Warn your coworkers informally so they all watch their step in the hallway.
opts.fb: Warning others is kind, but the incident still needs to go to your supervisor and be reported.

questions.q: Which of these are serious incidents that you tell your supervisor about immediately? Select all that apply.

opts.t: An event likely to put a worker in hospital
opts.fb: Yes. Likely hospital admission makes an incident serious.

opts.t: An uncontrolled fire or flood that may cause serious injury
opts.fb: Yes. Uncontrolled fires, floods or explosions that may cause serious injury are serious incidents.

opts.t: Part of a building's ceiling or structure gives way
opts.fb: Yes. Collapse or failure of part of a building is a serious incident.

opts.t: A colleague twists an ankle, gets first aid and finishes the day
opts.fb: Report it, but it isn't a serious incident unless it's likely to mean a hospital admission.

questions.src: Working Safely (U of A HSE) — Serious and potentially serious incidents
questions.fb: Serious incidents include death, likely hospital admission, uncontrolled fires, floods or explosions, and structural failures. A potentially serious incident is one that might have caused any of these.

questions.q: A potentially serious incident happens in your work area. Besides telling your supervisor immediately, what should you do?
