opts.t: Email hse.info@ualberta.ca and wait for HSE to reply before doing anything else.
opts.fb: Email isn't immediate. Serious and potentially serious incidents need a call to the Control Centre.

opts.t: Include it in your team's end-of-week summary for the manager.
opts.fb: These incidents must be reported immediately, not at the end of the week.

questions.src: Working Safely (U of A HSE) — Serious and potentially serious incidents

questions.q: A visitor at your service desk shouts and swears at you when you explain a policy, then leaves. You're shaken but not hurt. What should you do?

opts.t: Tell your supervisor and report it promptly, like any incident
opts.fb: Right. Prompt reporting of all incidents, including harassment and abuse, helps everyone stay safe.

opts.t: Let it go, since difficult visitors come with service work
opts.fb: Abuse isn't part of the job. Unreported, it can escalate and hurt the next person at the desk.

opts.t: Wait, and report it if the same visitor comes back and does it again
opts.fb: Waiting can let the behaviour escalate. Report it now.

questions.src: Working Safely (U of A HSE) — What about less obvious hazards?

questions.q: Your team is reviewing this week's events. Besides injuries, which should go to your supervisor and into an incident report? Select all that apply.

opts.t: A near miss or unsafe condition
opts.fb: Yes. Near misses and unsafe conditions are reported.

opts.t: Property damage
opts.fb: Yes. Property damage is on the list.

opts.t: A collision or other vehicle-related incident
opts.fb: Yes. Vehicle incidents are reported.

opts.t: Exposure to a hazardous substance
opts.fb: Yes. Exposures are reported.

opts.t: A planned fire drill that went smoothly
opts.fb: No. A planned drill that went as intended isn't an incident.

questions.src: Working Safely (U of A HSE) — What else should be reported?
questions.fb: Report injuries, exposures, near misses or unsafe conditions, vehicle incidents, spills and property damage to your supervisor and in an incident report.

questions.q: Coffee has spilled across the floor by the kitchenette door. Nobody's hurt, and you're due in a meeting in two minutes. What do you do?

opts.t: Clean it up now, or tell your supervisor right away if you can't
opts.fb: Right. Cleaning a spill right away, or reporting it as soon as possible, stops the next person from slipping.

opts.t: Leave it for the cleaning staff on their evening round
opts.fb: Hours of foot traffic could pass before then. Clean it up or report it now.

opts.t: Mention it to the next person you see so they can warn others
opts.fb: Word of mouth misses people. Clean it up, or report it to your supervisor.

questions.src: Working Safely (U of A HSE) — Is reporting that important? (spill scenario)

questions.q: You're at a meeting in a North Campus building when a colleague collapses and isn't responding. Who do you call?

opts.t: 911, then U of A Protective Services at 780-492-5050
opts.fb: Right. On a U of A campus other than ESQ, call 911 first, then UAPS, available 24/7. At ESQ, your second call is ESQ Security (780-428-1541).

opts.t: UAPS first, and let them decide whether to call 911
opts.fb: 911 comes first. Don't delay emergency services. At ESQ, your second call is ESQ Security (780-428-1541).

opts.t: Your supervisor first, then HSE by email after that
opts.fb: A life-safety emergency needs 911 right away, then UAPS. At ESQ, your second call is ESQ Security (780-428-1541).

questions.src: Working Safely (U of A HSE) — What if something goes wrong?; Emergency preparedness

questions.q: You want your team to be ready before an emergency happens. Which of these are readiness actions? Select all that apply.

opts.t: Find out where the nearest first aid kit and AED are
opts.fb: Yes. Knowing where emergency equipment is, and how to use it, is readiness.

opts.t: Install the MyUAlberta app and turn on its notifications
opts.fb: Yes. Working Safely lists this as a readiness action.

opts.t: Save UAPS's number to call first, before 911
opts.fb: 911 comes first. On a U of A campus other than ESQ, UAPS is your second call. At ESQ, your second call is ESQ Security (780-428-1541).

opts.t: Wait for HSE to schedule your team's evacuation plan review
opts.fb: Your team schedules its own review of the fire evacuation plan. That's part of readiness.

questions.src: Working Safely (U of A HSE) — How do I reduce the impact?
questions.fb: Readiness means plan and practise: know your emergency equipment, set up MyUAlberta notifications, and review your evacuation plan with your team.

questions.q: Your building reopens after an emergency closure, and some equipment in your office is damaged. What does the recovery phase ask you to do?

opts.t: Follow the continuity plan and report damage to your supervisor.
opts.fb: Right. Recovery means following your operational continuity plan to return to work, and reporting damages to your supervisor.

opts.t: Return to work as usual and replace the items on your own.
opts.fb: Damages should be reported to your supervisor, not handled quietly on your own.

opts.t: Stay home until HSE personally calls each team member to say it's safe.
opts.fb: Recovery is guided by your unit's operational continuity plan, which aims to return to work as soon as possible.

questions.src: Working Safely (U of A HSE) — What happens after an emergency?

questions.q: A colleague is being bullied and wants to raise it confidentially. Where does Working Safely point staff?

opts.t: The Office of Safe Disclosure and Human Rights, or their HR Partner
opts.fb: Right. For confidential psychological safety concerns, staff can go to the Office of Safe Disclosure and Human Rights or their HR Partner.

opts.t: UAPS at 780-492-5050, since bullying is mainly a campus security issue
opts.fb: UAPS handles emergencies such as life safety or a crime in progress. Confidential bullying concerns go to Safe Disclosure and Human Rights or HR.

opts.t: The chair of the Joint Health and Safety Committee
opts.fb: The JHSC resolves safety issues, but the course names Safe Disclosure and Human Rights or your HR Partner for confidential concerns.

questions.src: Working Safely (U of A HSE) — Emergency preparedness (where to report)

questions.q: Your team had a near miss this morning. No one was hurt and the situation is stable. How should it be reported?

opts.t: Tell your supervisor, then use the U of A incident report form
opts.fb: Right. Near misses are incidents, reported to your supervisor and through the university's incident report form.

opts.t: Call UAPS so there's an official record of what happened
opts.fb: UAPS handles emergencies such as life safety or a crime in progress, not near-miss records.

opts.t: Contact the Office of Safe Disclosure and Human Rights
opts.fb: That office handles confidential concerns such as bullying or harassment, not near misses.

questions.src: Working Safely (U of A HSE) — Emergency preparedness (where to report)

questions.q: You're working in a North Campus building. A shelving unit collapses in a storage room and a colleague is hurt. Which actions are part of the response? Select all that apply.

opts.t: Call 911, then UAPS at 780-492-5050
opts.fb: Yes. On a U of A campus other than ESQ, that's the first response. At ESQ, your second call is ESQ Security (780-428-1541).

opts.t: Call the Control Centre (780-492-5555) and ask for HSE On Call
opts.fb: Yes. Serious incidents also go to HSE On Call through the Control Centre.

opts.t: Report it on the U of A incident report form
opts.fb: Yes. Reporting is part of the response.

opts.t: Call UAPS first, so they can decide whether 911 is needed
opts.fb: 911 comes first, then UAPS. At ESQ, your second call is ESQ Security (780-428-1541).

opts.t: Hold off on any reports until things are back to normal
opts.fb: No. Reporting is part of the response, not something to leave until later.

questions.src: Working Safely (U of A HSE) — What if something goes wrong?; Serious and potentially serious incidents
questions.fb: On a campus other than ESQ: 911, then UAPS; tell your supervisor, call HSE On Call through the Control Centre, and report it. At ESQ, your second call is ESQ Security (780-428-1541).

questions.q: You have a non-urgent question about whether a workplace hazard in your area is being handled properly. Which contact fits best?

opts.t: Email HSE at hse.info@ualberta.ca
opts.fb: Right. Working Safely points to hse.info@ualberta.ca for advice on workplace hazard concerns.

opts.t: Call UAPS at 780-492-5050 to log the concern
opts.fb: UAPS handles emergencies such as life safety or a crime in progress.

opts.t: Call WCB to ask whether the hazard is covered
opts.fb: WCB deals with reported work injuries and illnesses, not hazard questions.

questions.src: Working Safely (U of A HSE) — Emergency preparedness (where to report)

questions.q: Your team is listing hazards in your work area. Which of these count as psychological hazards? Select all that apply.

opts.t: Fatigue
opts.fb: Yes. Fatigue is listed as a psychological hazard.

opts.t: Working alone
opts.fb: Yes. Working alone is listed, with separate Working Alone guidelines.

opts.t: Shift work
opts.fb: Yes. Shift work is listed as a psychological hazard.

opts.t: A loose ladder step
opts.fb: No. A broken ladder is a physical hazard, though it should still be reported.

opts.t: An oil spill on the floor
opts.fb: No. A spill is a physical slip hazard.

questions.src: Working Safely (U of A HSE) — Psychological hazards
questions.fb: Psychological hazards are workplace stressors that affect mental health and well-being, such as fatigue, shift work, bullying, violence and working alone.

questions.q: A colleague says bullying is a personal matter, so it doesn't belong in safety conversations. What's accurate?

opts.t: It's a psychological hazard, handled like physical ones
opts.fb: Right. Psychological hazards, like physical ones, are identified, assessed and controlled.

opts.t: It's a personal issue, best handled privately by those involved
opts.fb: Under the OHS Act, psychological hazards are workplace safety issues, not just personal ones.

opts.t: It becomes a safety issue once a formal written complaint is filed
opts.fb: Psychological hazards are identified and assessed proactively, not only after a complaint.

questions.src: Working Safely (U of A HSE) — What are psychological hazards?

questions.q: In meetings, a coworker keeps mocking a colleague's accent, and the colleague looks humiliated. What can you do?

opts.t: Check in with your colleague and report it: it can be harassment
opts.fb: Right. Unwelcome comments meant to degrade or humiliate can be harassment. Report it to your supervisor or, confidentially, the Office of Safe Disclosure and Human Rights.

opts.t: Leave it, as long as the comments are framed as friendly jokes
opts.fb: Framing doesn't change the effect. Unwelcome comments that humiliate someone can be harassment.

opts.t: Wait until the comments show up in writing before reporting them
opts.fb: Harassment includes spoken comments and actions, not just written messages.

questions.src: Working Safely (U of A HSE) — Harassment and bullying; Emergency preparedness (where to report)

questions.q: Your supervisor meets you privately to give constructive feedback about several missed deadlines. Is this bullying?

opts.t: No. Evaluating performance and giving feedback are not bullying.
opts.fb: Right. Working Safely says evaluating performance and constructive feedback are not bullying.

opts.t: Yes, because the conversation made you feel uncomfortable and singled out.
opts.fb: Feedback can be uncomfortable without being bullying. These actions are within a supervisor's authority.

opts.t: Yes, unless someone from HR is also present at the meeting.
opts.fb: HR doesn't need to be present. Constructive feedback given in private is a legitimate supervisor action.

questions.src: Working Safely (U of A HSE) — Harassment and bullying

questions.q: A teammate says any tough conversation with a supervisor counts as bullying. Which supervisor actions are NOT bullying? Select all that apply.

opts.t: Enforcing workplace policies and procedures
opts.fb: Yes. Enforcing policies is part of a supervisor's authority.

opts.t: Denying training or leave with good reason
opts.fb: Yes. A denial with good reason isn't bullying.

opts.t: Criticizing someone in front of the team to make an example of them
opts.fb: No. Public hostility that disrespects someone fits the description of bullying.

opts.t: Hinting at a demotion to pressure someone into extra work
opts.fb: No. Threats and intimidation, including abuse of power, are bullying.

questions.src: Working Safely (U of A HSE) — Harassment and bullying
questions.fb: Supervisors may enforce policies, evaluate performance, give feedback, deny requests with good reason, and discuss discipline privately. Hostility, threats and abuse of power are bullying.

questions.q: Which situation is an example of workplace bullying?

opts.t: A coworker deliberately withholds information you need to do your job.
opts.fb: Right. Deliberate acts that interfere with the target's work are a form of workplace bullying.

opts.t: Your supervisor turns down a leave request for a clear business reason.
opts.fb: Denying leave with good reason is a legitimate supervisor action, not bullying.

opts.t: A colleague politely disagrees with your proposal during a meeting.
opts.fb: Respectful disagreement isn't bullying. Bullying involves hostility, intimidation or deliberate interference.

questions.src: Working Safely (U of A HSE) — Harassment and bullying

questions.title: What do you say?
questions.q: Your manager often announces changes without warning, and you're not sure how your project fits the team's goals. You have a one-on-one with your manager this week. What do you say?

opts.t: "Could you help me see how my project fits the team's goals, and what changes might be coming?"
opts.fb: Right. Clear leadership and expectations is one of the 13 psychosocial factors. Asking questions, and two-way communication, help.

opts.t: "Everything's fine on my end."
opts.fb: Unclear expectations create unease. It's fair to ask; communication should go both ways.

opts.t: "Could we save the bigger picture for my annual review?"
opts.fb: Clarity needs regular check-ins, not a once-a-year conversation.

questions.src: Psychologically Safe Workplaces — 13 factors (Clear leadership and expectations)

questions.title: What do you say?
questions.q: A teammate spent weeks on a workshop design that leadership has now shelved. You see them in the kitchen. What do you say?

opts.t: "I know the design's been shelved, but thank you. The weeks you put into those activities really showed."
opts.fb: Right. Recognition means acknowledging effort fairly and promptly, including on projects that get shelved.

opts.t: "Shame it didn't go ahead. On to the next one."
opts.fb: Recognition covers effort, not only outcomes. A specific thank-you matters here.

opts.t: "We should put you up for the year-end team awards."
opts.fb: Recognition works best when it's prompt and specific, not saved for a formal program.

questions.src: Psychologically Safe Workplaces — 13 factors (Recognition and reward)
questions.note: Distractor "say nothing" rendered as moving on without acknowledging the effort.

questions.title: What do you say?
questions.q: A colleague tells you they've been having a hard time and asks where U of A staff can find support right away. What do you say?

opts.t: "The Culture of Care page links to Immediate Resources to Get Help Now, through EFAP. Want me to send you the link?"
opts.fb: Right. The Culture of Care page links staff and faculty to immediate resources through the Employee and Family Assistance Program.

opts.t: "You could bring it to the next Joint Health and Safety Committee meeting."
opts.fb: The JHSC resolves workplace safety issues. Personal support is available right away through EFAP.

opts.t: "Try the Workers' Compensation Board claims line."
opts.fb: WCB deals with reported work injuries and illnesses. EFAP is the place for immediate support.

questions.src: A Culture of Care — More resources

questions.title: What do you say?
questions.q: A teammate has been put on three back-to-back projects with no time to finish any of them. They tell you about it over coffee. What do you say?

opts.t: "That's a lot. Could you raise it with our lead and agree on priorities?"
opts.fb: Right. Workload management means tasks can realistically be done in the time available. Agreeing priorities, and cutting what isn't needed, helps.

opts.t: "Hang in there, and bring it up at your performance review."
opts.fb: Months of overload is a psychosocial hazard. Raise it now.

opts.t: "Send me some of it. I'll work on it at home tonight."
opts.fb: That moves the overload onto you without fixing it. Raise the workload with your lead.

questions.src: Psychologically Safe Workplaces — 13 factors (Workload management)

questions.title: What do you say?
questions.q: After the meeting, the new coordinator tells you she spotted the error but didn't want to embarrass anyone. What do you say?

opts.t: "Thanks for telling me. I'll fix it now, and please feel free to raise things like this in the meeting. We'd all rather know."
opts.fb: Right. Psychological safety means people can speak up about mistakes without being punished or humiliated. Thanking her makes the next time easier.

opts.t: "Thanks. Let's just fix it quietly so nobody's embarrassed."
opts.fb: Fixing it is good, but quietly working around it teaches the team that mistakes stay hidden.

opts.t: "Good catch, but errors like that should go to the team lead privately."
opts.fb: Routing everything privately signals that raising issues openly isn't safe.

questions.src: A Culture of Care — Safety definitions (psychological safety); Psychologically Safe Workplaces — Organizational culture

questions.title: What do you say?
questions.q: After a Tuesday team call, Priya stays on and tells you quietly that she's been struggling for a few weeks and today is a bad day. What do you say?

opts.t: "I'll let our manager know what's going on so they can step in."
opts.fb: Her story is her personal information. Keeping it confidential is a basic form of respect, so let her decide who else hears it.

opts.t: "Thank you for telling me. I'm here to listen. If it helps, there's also the EFAP Immediate Resources page."
opts.fb: Right. Feeling supported on hard days is the goal, and you don't need to be an expert. The Immediate Resources to Get Help Now (EFAP) page is there for staff.

opts.t: "It sounds like it could be burnout. Maybe ask your doctor about that?"
opts.fb: It's not your role to guess at what's going on. Listening and pointing to support is enough, and safer for both of you.

questions.src: Psychologically Safe Workplaces — Video takeaways 1 (Psychological Support) and 4 (Civility & Respect); Culture of Care — More Resources (Immediate Resources to Get Help Now)
questions.note: SME: the "burnout" distractor gives a concrete example of guessing at a cause; swap for a vaguer line if naming a condition is a concern.

questions.q: Your team wants to make it easier to talk about mental health at work. Which of these fit the guidance? Select all that apply.

opts.t: Treat mental health as part of everyday health talk
opts.fb: Yes. Normalizing mental health alongside physical health is named as a good first step in reducing stigma.

opts.t: Remind each other what benefits and EFAP cover
opts.fb: Yes. Sharing what benefits and EFAP offer is one of the listed practices, and colleagues can do it too.

opts.t: Avoid the topic so no one feels singled out
opts.fb: Silence tends to keep stigma in place. The aim is for people to talk about mental health without stigma.

opts.t: Wait to raise it until someone is clearly in crisis
opts.fb: The university's approach is proactive: address mental health early, before problems develop.

questions.fb: Reducing stigma starts early and in everyday conversation, not only in a crisis.
questions.src: Psychologically Safe Workplaces — Video takeaway 1 (Psychological Support); Culture of Care — Workplace Mental Health + Well-Being Action Plan

questions.q: Before Friday's workshop debrief, you realize a link you set up sent 12 people to the wrong registration form. No one has noticed yet. What do you do?

opts.t: Fix it quietly and move on
opts.fb: Fixing it is good, but hiding it means the team can't learn from it. Where mistakes stay hidden, trust erodes.

opts.t: Raise it at the debrief and say how you'll fix it
opts.fb: Right. Safe voice means mistakes can be raised without fear, and modelling it helps others do the same.

opts.t: Wait to see whether anyone is affected
opts.fb: Waiting lets the problem grow and keeps it hidden. Raising it early is what a trusting culture depends on.

questions.src: Psychologically Safe Workplaces — Video takeaway 2 (Organizational Culture); Culture of Care — Safety Definitions (psychological safety)

questions.title: What do you say?
questions.q: In a planning meeting, Jae raises a concern about the new intake process. Another colleague sighs, "Here we go again." Jae goes quiet. What do you say?

opts.t: "Jae, I'd like to hear more. Can you go on?"
opts.fb: Right. A small act like this keeps safe voice alive. Culture is shaped by each person's behaviour, not just policies.

opts.t: "Let's keep moving. Jae, we can talk after the meeting."
opts.fb: Following up is kind, but the team loses the concern and learns that raising things gets shut down.

opts.t: (To the lead) "Over to you. It's your meeting."
opts.fb: Leaders play a big role, but policies and training alone can't change culture. Everyone's behaviour counts.

questions.src: Psychologically Safe Workplaces — Video takeaway 2 (Organizational Culture)
questions.note: Distractor "stay out of it; culture is up to leaders" rendered as handing it to the lead, so it can be a spoken line.

questions.title: What do you say?
questions.q: You leave a project kickoff unsure what "done" looks like for your part of the new onboarding module. What do you say?

opts.t: (To your lead) "I'll take a best guess and adjust when you've seen it."
opts.fb: Guessing risks rework and stress. Being unsure of your role is a known source of unease, so clear it up early.

opts.t: (To a teammate) "What do you think the lead meant by 'done' for my part?"
opts.fb: A teammate may be just as unsure. Communication should go both ways with the person setting the direction.

opts.t: (To your lead) "Can I summarize my part back to you, to check I've got what 'done' looks like?"
opts.fb: Right. Summarizing the direction back is a way to check understanding, and you should feel safe asking.

questions.src: Psychologically Safe Workplaces — Video takeaway 3 (Clear Leadership & Expectations)
questions.note: The options go to different people, so each has a bracketed cue.

questions.title: What do you say?
questions.q: In the shared workroom, Owen starts telling a few people about a coworker's upcoming medical appointment, which he overheard on her phone. What do you say?

opts.t: "Oh, I hope it's nothing serious."
opts.fb: Joining in, even kindly, keeps it going. Good intentions don't change the impact: her health information is personal, and sharing it isn't his call.

opts.t: "Owen, that's hers to share. Let's keep it to ourselves."
opts.fb: Right. Protecting the confidentiality of personal information is a basic form of respect at work.

opts.t: "Maybe just keep it within our team, Owen."
opts.fb: A smaller audience is still sharing personal information without her consent.

questions.src: Psychologically Safe Workplaces — Video takeaway 4 (Civility & Respect)
questions.note: Distractor "let it go; he means well" rendered as a sympathetic reply that lets the sharing continue.

questions.q: A Teams thread about a workshop design is turning sarcastic between you and a colleague who disagrees with your approach. What's the best move?

opts.t: Reply in the same tone so they see how it feels
opts.fb: Matching the tone escalates the conflict. Respect has to be modelled to spread.

opts.t: Suggest a quick call and keep it to the ideas
opts.fb: Right. Treating differences as discussions, not battles, is a sign of a respectful workplace, and talking live often helps.

opts.t: Drop out of the thread and let others decide
opts.fb: Stepping away leaves the conflict unresolved. Resolving conflicts quickly is part of civility and respect.

questions.src: Psychologically Safe Workplaces — Video takeaways 2 (Organizational Culture) and 4 (Civility & Respect)

questions.title: What do you say?
questions.q: Last time you gave Tomás feedback on his slides, he got visibly upset. You're reviewing his next deck today and see him beforehand. What do you say?

opts.t: "Looks good. No notes this time."
opts.fb: Avoiding feedback doesn't help him grow. The guidance is to adjust how you give it, not to stop.

opts.t: "I'll send my comments in writing so you can go through them on your own."
opts.fb: That might suit him, or it might not. Rather than guessing, ask how he prefers to receive it.

opts.t: "Before I review it, how do you like to get feedback: in person, in writing, or a mix?"
opts.fb: Right. Asking how someone prefers feedback, then delivering it that way consistently, is the approach the guidance describes.

questions.src: Psychologically Safe Workplaces — Video takeaway 5 (Psychological Competencies & Requirements)

questions.title: What do you say?
questions.q: Your role is changing, and you'll now handle tense conversations with unhappy clients at the service desk. You don't feel ready for that part yet. Your lead asks how you're feeling about the change. What do you say?

opts.t: "I'm keen, but I don't feel ready for the tense client conversations yet. Could I get some training for that part?"
opts.fb: Right. When a job changes, the skills it needs should be made clear, and staff oriented and trained to build them.

opts.t: "All good. I'll figure it out as I go."
opts.fb: Learning on the fly with difficult clients adds stress. Training and support for those roles is part of the guidance.

opts.t: "That part wasn't in my original job, so I'd rather not take it on."
opts.fb: Roles do change. The better step is to ask for the support to do the new part well.

questions.src: Psychologically Safe Workplaces — Video takeaways 4 (Civility & Respect) and 5 (Psychological Competencies & Requirements)

questions.q: You want to build your facilitation skills, but there's no training budget this year. Which options fit no-cost growth? Select all that apply.

opts.t: Shadow a senior facilitator at a workshop
opts.fb: Yes. Job shadowing is one of the everyday, no-cost options named.

opts.t: Watch a webinar with a colleague and talk it over
opts.fb: Yes. Attending a webinar together is listed as a no-cost way to grow.

opts.t: Ask for a career conversation with your lead
opts.fb: Yes. Career conversations count as growth and cost nothing.

opts.t: Wait until there's budget for a formal course
opts.fb: Growth doesn't require a big budget. It can happen every day at no cost.

opts.t: Only count courses that give a certificate
opts.fb: Mentoring, shared articles and shadowing all count. Development isn't limited to formal credentials.

questions.fb: Growth can happen every day without a budget: shadowing, webinars, mentoring and career conversations.
questions.src: Psychologically Safe Workplaces — Video takeaway 6 (Growth & Development)

questions.title: What do you say?
questions.q: You've found a free webinar on accessible slide design next Wednesday. Mei joined the team three weeks ago. What do you say?

opts.t: "Mei, I've signed you up for a webinar next Wednesday. You'll like it."
opts.fb: Signing her up takes the choice away. People differ in readiness, so ask first.

opts.t: (To a teammate) "I won't mention it to Mei. She's new and has enough on."
opts.fb: Assuming for her may mean a missed chance. Offer it and let her decide.

opts.t: "Mei, there's a free webinar on accessible slide design next Wednesday. Would you like to join me?"
opts.fb: Right. People's readiness varies with career and life stage, so ask before offering an opportunity.

questions.src: Psychologically Safe Workplaces — Video takeaway 6 (Growth & Development)

questions.title: What do you say?
questions.q: Aisha spent two evenings sorting the shared workshop-materials drive, and you found what you needed in seconds this morning. What do you say?

opts.t: "Aisha, thank you for sorting the shared drive. I found what I needed in seconds this morning."
opts.fb: Right. Specific, prompt thanks that links effort to impact is what makes recognition meaningful.

opts.t: "Great work, everyone!"
opts.fb: General praise misses the specific effort. Recognition works best when it names what the person did.

opts.t: "Let's remember this for the team awards at the end of the year."
opts.fb: Recognition should be timely. Catching people doing something right, when it happens, matters more than formal programs.

questions.src: Psychologically Safe Workplaces — Factor 7 definition; Video takeaway 7 (Recognition & Reward)

questions.title: What do you say?
questions.q: You're helping plan a thank-you for the team after a busy fall term. Someone suggests a group escape-room outing as the reward. What do you say?

opts.t: "Sounds fun. Most people would enjoy it, so let's book it."
opts.fb: Most isn't everyone. Rewards don't motivate everyone equally, so a one-size choice can leave people out.

opts.t: "Could we ask the team what kind of thanks they'd value first?"
opts.fb: Right. The guidance is to find out what actually motivates your people rather than assume.

opts.t: "Let's keep it a surprise."
opts.fb: A surprise rules out checking what people want, and the choice might not suit some of them.

questions.src: Psychologically Safe Workplaces — Video takeaways 7 (Recognition & Reward) and 10 (Engagement)

questions.title: What do you say?
questions.q: Your lead shares a draft of a new booking process for the workshop calendar and asks for input by Thursday. You use it daily and think two steps add nothing. What do you say?

opts.t: (To your lead) "I use this daily, and I think two of the steps could go. Can I suggest a simpler way?"
opts.fb: Right. Leadership sets what needs doing, and staff have input into how they do their own work.

opts.t: (To your lead) "Looks fine. Process is really leadership's call."
opts.fb: You were asked for input on how the work is done, which is exactly where staff influence matters.

opts.t: (To a teammate) "I'll go along with it for now, but between us, two of those steps are pointless."
opts.fb: Side conversations don't change the process. Input helps most when it reaches the person deciding.

questions.src: Psychologically Safe Workplaces — Video takeaway 8 (Involvement & Influence)

questions.q: An anonymous team pulse survey arrives. A colleague says, "Just give everything top marks so we don't look bad." How do you answer it?

opts.t: Give top marks so the team looks good
opts.fb: Inflated answers hide real issues, so nothing gets fixed. The survey only helps if it reflects reality.

opts.t: Skip it, since surveys rarely change anything
opts.fb: Surveys are meant to be acted on, and your input is part of how work improves.

opts.t: Answer honestly, including what needs work
opts.fb: Right. Honest input is how staff take part in decisions, and it gives leaders something real to act on.

questions.src: Psychologically Safe Workplaces — Video takeaways 2 (Organizational Culture) and 8 (Involvement & Influence)
questions.note: The source's survey guidance is written for managers (ask only what you'll act on, respond promptly). The staff action (answer honestly) is inferred from it. SME: please confirm the framing.

questions.title: What do you say?
questions.q: You spend about three hours each month on a usage report, and as far as you can tell no one reads it. You have a check-in with your lead today. What do you say?

opts.t: "Just so you know, I've stopped doing the usage report."
opts.fb: Dropping it on your own could leave someone without data they need. Agree on the change first.

opts.t: "Is the monthly usage report still needed? It takes about three hours, and I'm not sure anyone uses it."
opts.fb: Right. Agreeing on priorities and cutting unnecessary tasks is part of good workload management. Reports nobody reads are the classic example.

opts.t: "Nothing new from me. The reports are all on track."
opts.fb: Good workload management is about working efficiently, not doing less. Asking about the report is a reasonable question, not a sign of laziness.

questions.src: Psychologically Safe Workplaces — Video takeaway 9 (Workload Management)
questions.note: Distractor "quietly stop sending it" rendered as announcing that you've already stopped (same logic: dropping it without agreement).

questions.title: What do you say?
questions.q: Two program leads have each asked you for a different task "first thing tomorrow." You can't do both well by then. You catch them both together. What do you say?

opts.t: "No problem. I'll stay late and get both done."
opts.fb: That might work once, but it drains your energy and hides the real problem: unclear priorities.

opts.t: (To the more senior lead) "I'll get yours done first, then the other one."
opts.fb: Guessing at priority can still leave someone let down. It's better to make the priority clear.

opts.t: "I can't do both well by tomorrow. Could you two agree on which comes first?"
opts.fb: Right. Unclear priorities are a named stressor, and agreeing on them is a key part of managing workload.

questions.src: Psychologically Safe Workplaces — Video takeaway 9 (Workload Management)

questions.title: What do you say?
questions.q: You and Ana are co-building a leadership workshop. You know she's a skilled visual designer, but she's been given only scheduling tasks. What do you say?

opts.t: "Ana, would you like to take on the slide design?"
opts.fb: Right. Knowing people's strengths and giving them chances to use them builds engagement.

opts.t: "Let's stick to the tasks as assigned so we don't step on toes."
opts.fb: Asking her doesn't overrule anyone. It invites her to use a strength she already has.

opts.t: "I'll just do the slides myself. It's faster."
opts.fb: That may save time today but misses a chance for her to feel her work matters.

questions.src: Psychologically Safe Workplaces — Video takeaway 10 (Engagement)

questions.q: Your team is planning ways to connect more this winter. Which ideas fit the guidance on engagement? Select all that apply.

opts.t: Offer a mix of group and one-on-one options
opts.fb: Yes. Some people prefer group activities and others prefer one-on-one conversations.

opts.t: Ask the team what they'd enjoy before planning
opts.fb: Yes. Asking for input is itself one of the ways to build engagement.

opts.t: Make the group event mandatory so it's fair
opts.fb: Requiring one format ignores that people connect in different ways.

opts.t: Pick one big activity that everyone does together
opts.fb: A single format won't suit everyone. Varied activities work better.

questions.fb: Engagement grows when people are asked for input and have varied ways to take part.
questions.src: Psychologically Safe Workplaces — Video takeaway 10 (Engagement)

questions.q: It's 10:45 PM on a Tuesday and you think of a question for your colleague about tomorrow's slides. It isn't urgent. What do you do?

opts.t: Send it now with "no rush"
opts.fb: Even with "no rush," a late-night ping can pull someone back into work. Balance means respecting personal time.

opts.t: Schedule it for the morning
opts.fb: Right. Supporting balance between work and personal life includes not pulling people into work after hours when it can wait.

opts.t: Send it now, since they can mute Teams
opts.fb: Putting the burden on them to block you doesn't support balance. Holding non-urgent messages does.

questions.src: Psychologically Safe Workplaces — Factor 11 definition (Balance); Video takeaway 9 (energy left for life outside work)
questions.note: The Balance video's content wasn't available in the summary; this item rests on the factor definition. SME: please confirm that the off-hours messaging practice fits U of A guidance.

questions.q: You're setting up a new weekly project check-in. Leila has mentioned she leaves at 3:30 on Mondays and Wednesdays for family. The time that suits you is Monday at 4:00. What do you do?

opts.t: Book Monday at 4:00 and send her the notes
opts.fb: Notes help, but she'd be left out of every meeting. A time that works for everyone supports balance.

opts.t: Find a time that works for everyone
opts.fb: Right. Recognizing and supporting balance between work and family demands is what this factor asks.

opts.t: Book it and let her ask if it doesn't work
opts.fb: She has already told you about the conflict. Making her push back puts the burden on her.

questions.src: Psychologically Safe Workplaces — Factor 11 definition (Balance)

questions.title: What do you say?
questions.q: Rosa tells you a teammate keeps making remarks about her religion. When she mentioned it, he said she was "too sensitive." What do you say?

opts.t: "Give it some time. He probably doesn't mean any harm."
opts.fb: Brushing it off is the kind of dismissal that leaves people feeling unsafe. The behaviour matters, whatever the intent.

opts.t: "I'm glad you told me, and it's not okay. The Office of Safe Disclosure and Human Rights or your HR Partner can help with this."
opts.fb: Right. When concerns are dismissed, people feel unsafe. The Office of Safe Disclosure and Human Rights and HR Partners are there for these concerns.

opts.t: "You should call him out at the next team meeting."
opts.fb: A public confrontation could escalate things. Fair processes that preserve everyone's dignity are the better route.

questions.src: Psychologically Safe Workplaces — Video takeaway 12 (Psychological Protection); Working Safely — Slide 49 (psychological safety concerns); Culture of Care — Cultural safety definition

questions.q: Which of these should you report to your supervisor rather than brush off? Select all that apply.

opts.t: A coworker's repeated jokes about a colleague's disability
opts.fb: Yes. Repeated demeaning comments can be harassment or discrimination, and should be reported promptly.

opts.t: A visitor telling you he'll "find out where you live"
opts.fb: Yes. Threats are a serious psychological protection issue. Report them promptly.

opts.t: A colleague shouting and slamming a binder at a teammate
opts.fb: Yes. Aggression like this is covered under psychological protection, and prompt reporting helps keep everyone safe.

opts.t: Your supervisor privately discussing your missed deadlines
opts.fb: Evaluating performance and giving constructive feedback in private aren't bullying.

opts.t: A colleague disagreeing with your idea in a meeting
opts.fb: Respectful disagreement is healthy. Differences treated as discussions are a sign of a respectful workplace.

questions.fb: Harassment, discrimination, threats and aggression get reported. Fair feedback and respectful disagreement don't.
questions.src: Psychologically Safe Workplaces — Video takeaways 4 and 12; Working Safely — Slides 16, 27, 28, 42

questions.q: Hana will run Thursday-evening workshops alone in the suite this term. She tells you she's anxious about being on her own after hours. What's the most helpful response?

opts.t: Reassure her that nothing has happened there before
opts.fb: Being told it's fine doesn't remove the worry. Expecting harm with no backup plan can itself cause psychological injury.

opts.t: Tell her the nerves will fade once she's done it a few times
opts.fb: The worry is a real concern, not just nerves. A plan reduces the distress that anticipation causes.

opts.t: Help her ask your lead for a check-in plan that suits her
opts.fb: Right. Regular check-ins and asking the affected worker what would help are the practices named for lone work.

questions.src: Psychologically Safe Workplaces — Video takeaway 13 (Protection of Physical Safety); Working Safely — Slide 26 (working alone as a psychological hazard)

questions.q: After a ceiling leak near her desk last month, Dev keeps worrying about mould. A couple of people have started teasing her about it. What do you do?

opts.t: Take it seriously and help her report it
opts.fb: Right. Fear of exposure can cause lasting distress, and confidence that it's been checked lowers that distress. Report conditions to your supervisor.

opts.t: Tell her it's probably nothing, so she can relax
opts.fb: You can't know that, and dismissing the worry won't ease it. Getting it checked will.

opts.t: Suggest she quietly move to another desk for now
opts.fb: Moving may ease her mind but leaves a possible hazard unreported for others.

questions.src: Psychologically Safe Workplaces — Video takeaway 13 (Protection of Physical Safety); Working Safely — Slide 16 (report unsafe conditions)

questions.q: Your unit just hosted a lunch-and-learn on managing stress. A colleague says, "Great, now we're a psychologically safe workplace." What's missing?

opts.t: Nothing. Awareness events are what make a workplace safe
opts.fb: Awareness and education promote mental health, which is the healthy side. Safe is about preventing harm.

opts.t: Safe also means preventing harm, not just promoting health
opts.fb: Right. A healthy workplace promotes mental health. A safe one prevents harm from negligent, reckless or deliberate conduct.

opts.t: Safe means no one ever feels uncomfortable or challenged at work
opts.fb: Respectful debate and tough feedback still happen in a safe workplace. The focus is on preventing harm.

questions.src: Psychologically Safe Workplaces — Overview, Key distinction

questions.title: What do you say?
questions.q: Marco is back Monday after several weeks on leave. Teammates are debating whether to ask him what happened. What do you say?

opts.t: (To Marco) "Welcome back! So, what happened? We were all wondering."
opts.fb: Asking puts him on the spot about personal information. Let him choose what, if anything, to share.

opts.t: (To your teammates) "Let's give him space and steer clear for a bit."
opts.fb: Keeping your distance can feel isolating. A supportive environment helps people recover and stay well.

opts.t: (To Marco) "Welcome back, Marco. It's good to have you here."
opts.fb: Right. A supportive welcome helps, and keeping personal information confidential is a basic form of respect. Let him decide what to share.

questions.src: Psychologically Safe Workplaces — Video takeaways 1 (Psychological Support) and 4 (Civility & Respect)

questions.q: You're booking an offsite venue for a team planning day. The best-priced room is up a flight of stairs with no elevator, and a teammate uses a mobility aid. What do you do?

opts.t: Choose a venue everyone can get into
opts.fb: Right. Cultural safety includes mobility. Everyone should be able to take part as who they are, without workarounds.

opts.t: Book it and help her up the stairs
opts.fb: That singles her out and adds physical risk. A step-free venue means no one has to be helped in.

opts.t: Book it and offer her a video link instead
opts.fb: That leaves her out of the in-person day. Every employee should feel accepted and included.

questions.src: Culture of Care — Safety Definitions (cultural safety; physical safety)

questions.q: A colleague has told the team he now goes by Sam and uses he/him. A few people keep using his old name "until the system updates." What do you do?

opts.t: Use his old name until the records change
opts.fb: The system can lag. How he identifies is what matters, and no one should have to mask who they are.

opts.t: Use Sam and he/him, and correct yourself if you slip
opts.fb: Right. Cultural safety means people are respected for who they are, including their gender identity.

opts.t: Avoid using his name or pronouns for now
opts.fb: Avoiding them is noticeable and can feel like rejection. Using what he's asked for is simple respect.

questions.src: Culture of Care — Safety Definitions (cultural safety)

questions.title: What do you say?
questions.q: Your team holds a lunch meeting every Friday at 12:30. Yusuf has mentioned he steps out at that time for prayer, so he keeps missing it. You help plan the meeting. What do you say?

opts.t: "No problem, Yusuf. We'll keep 12:30 and I'll fill you in afterwards."
opts.fb: He'd keep missing the discussion. No one should have to choose between their faith and being part of the team.

opts.t: "Could you pray a bit earlier on Fridays so you can make it?"
opts.fb: That asks him to change his practice to fit the meeting. Cultural safety means not having to mask who you are.

opts.t: "What time on Fridays would work for you? I'd like to find one that fits."
opts.fb: Right. Respecting faith as part of who someone is includes simple adjustments like meeting times.

questions.src: Culture of Care — Safety Definitions (cultural safety)

questions.title: What do you say?
questions.q: In the lunchroom, a colleague takes a call from family in Spanish. Someone nearby says, "English only in here, please." What do you say?

opts.t: "She's on a call with family. Speaking Spanish is fine here."
opts.fb: Right. Employees are diverse linguistically and culturally, and no one should have to mask that at work. Check in with her afterwards too.

opts.t: "Fair enough, it is a shared space."
opts.fb: Going along with the comment signals agreement. A Culture of Care means everyone helps make the space safe.

opts.t: (To your colleague) "Maybe take personal calls outside next time?"
opts.fb: That asks her to hide part of who she is. The comment is the problem, not her call.

questions.src: Culture of Care — Safety Definitions (cultural safety)
questions.note: Distractor "stay out of it" can't be spoken, so it became going along with the comment (same logic: not speaking up). SME: confirm the bracketed stage direction is acceptable in a dialogue option.

questions.title: What do you say?
questions.q: You're in a planning meeting and have a question you worry sounds basic. What do you say?

opts.t: "Nothing from me. I'll look it up later."
opts.fb: Others may have the same question. A team is safer when people can ask without fear of looking foolish.

opts.t: "This might be a basic one, but can you explain how the sign-up step works?"
opts.fb: Right. Psychological safety is the belief that you won't be punished or humiliated for asking questions, and asking helps build it.

opts.t: "Nothing for now. I'll catch someone after the meeting."
opts.fb: That can work, but the group misses the question. Asking openly helps build a team where questions are safe.

questions.src: Culture of Care — Safety Definitions (psychological safety)

questions.title: What do you say?
questions.q: You wake up Wednesday with a fever and sore throat. You're scheduled to co-facilitate an in-person workshop at 9:00. You call your co-facilitator. What do you say?

opts.t: "I've got a fever, so I'll come in masked and keep my distance."
opts.fb: A mask helps, but the guidance is clear: if you're unwell, stay home.

opts.t: "I'll run the workshop with you, then go straight home."
opts.fb: You'd still be spending hours with participants. Staying home keeps the community healthy.

opts.t: "I'm unwell, so I'm staying home today. Can we sort out how you'll cover?"
opts.fb: Right. Stay home when unwell, take care of yourself and follow public health guidelines. Telling people early lets them cover.

questions.src: Culture of Care — More Resources (Stay Home when Unwell)

questions.q: At a hot desk, you notice the universal power adaptor someone left plugged in is cracked and feels warm. What do you do?

opts.t: Use a different outlet and leave the adaptor be
opts.fb: The next person may use it. Damaged equipment should come out of service and be reported.

opts.t: Unplug it if safe and tell your supervisor
opts.fb: Right. Damaged equipment comes out of service, and unsafe conditions are reported to your supervisor.

opts.t: Tape over the crack so it's safe to keep using
opts.fb: Tape doesn't fix a damaged electrical part. Electrical repairs need qualified people.

questions.src: Culture of Care — News: Incident Lessons Learned: Damaged Universal Power Adaptor (headline); Working Safely — Slides 16 and 33 (take defective equipment out of service); Culture of Care — News: Electrical Incidents (headline)
questions.note: The Culture of Care page only gives the news headline. The correct answer rests on Working Safely (take defective equipment out of service; report unsafe conditions). SME: please confirm it matches the incident's lessons.

questions.q: In January, a colleague slips on slush just inside the suite entrance. She catches herself on the wall and says she's fine. Which of these should happen? Select all that apply.

opts.t: Check that she's really OK
opts.fb: Yes. Respond to any injury first and get help if needed.

opts.t: Clean up or flag the wet spot so the next person doesn't slip
opts.fb: Yes. The best fix is to deal with the hazard right away. If you can't, report it as soon as possible.

opts.t: Tell your supervisor and file an incident report
opts.fb: Yes. Once things are stable, report it, even if there's no injury. It may be a near miss.

opts.t: Skip the report, since she wasn't hurt
opts.fb: Near misses get reported too. In the Working Safely example, an unreported slip led to a worse fall for the next person.

opts.t: Leave it for caretaking to notice on their rounds
opts.fb: Someone else could slip in the meantime. Safety is everyone's responsibility.

questions.fb: After a slip: check on the person, fix or flag the hazard, and report it, even with no injury.
questions.src: Working Safely — Slides 34, 39–40 (Nick and Carlos slip scenario); Culture of Care — News: Not slipping up on slips and falls (headline)
questions.note: The Culture of Care news item is a headline only. The answer is built on Working Safely. SME: please confirm it matches the slips-and-falls guidance.

questions.q: You're not a supervisor, but you'd like to be a Safety Champion on your team. Which are realistic ways to start? Select all that apply.

opts.t: Lead a short safety moment at a team meeting
opts.fb: Yes. Leading the next safety moment at a staff meeting is one of the suggested ways to lead by example.

opts.t: Share what was learned from a recent near miss
opts.fb: Yes. Sharing learnings from incidents helps the whole unit improve.

opts.t: Wait until you're named to a safety committee
opts.fb: Anyone can be a Safety Champion by keeping themselves and others safe. No appointment needed.

opts.t: Thank a teammate for a smart safety idea
opts.fb: Yes. Celebrating safety successes and recognizing safe behaviour is part of promoting safety.

opts.t: Take over your supervisor's inspection duties
opts.fb: You can take part in inspections, but running them is the supervisor's role. Start with what you can do day to day.

questions.fb: Safety Champions integrate safety into everyday work: share lessons, lead safety moments, recognize safe ideas.
questions.src: Culture of Care — Resources for Safety Champions; Working Safely — Slide 55 (Lead by example, Share learnings)

questions.q: Setting up for a Tuesday workshop, Priya trips over a stack of boxes and cuts her forearm on a table edge. It's bleeding steadily. What do you do first?

opts.t: Get her first aid or medical help as needed
opts.fb: Right. Responding to injuries comes first, and you get medical help as needed before anything else.

opts.t: Move the boxes so the next person doesn't trip
opts.fb: Protecting the scene matters, but it comes after you respond to the injury.

opts.t: Call your supervisor and start the incident report
opts.fb: Tell your supervisor and report once the situation is stable. Priya's injury needs attention first.

questions.src: Working Safely 2023 — Slide 34, In case of an incident

questions.q: Priya's cut is bandaged and she's resting. The boxes are still in the doorway, and participants will arrive in 15 minutes. What's your next step?

opts.t: Leave everything as it is so nobody disturbs the evidence
opts.fb: Preserving evidence matters, but leaving a trip hazard in a busy doorway invites a second incident.

opts.t: Keep people clear of the spot, then tell your supervisor
opts.fb: Right. Protect the scene to prevent a secondary incident, then tell your supervisor and report once things are stable.

opts.t: Run the workshop and report it at Friday's team meeting
opts.fb: Once the situation is stable, you tell your supervisor and report. Waiting days isn't the process.

questions.src: Working Safely 2023 — Slide 34, In case of an incident

questions.q: On Thursday afternoon, a coat rack in the shared workroom tips over and cracks a colleague's monitor. Nobody is hurt. What should you do? Select all that apply.

opts.t: Keep people back from the area until it's safe
opts.fb: Yes. Protecting the scene helps prevent secondary incidents and further damage.

opts.t: Leave the rack and monitor where they fell for now
opts.fb: Yes. Protecting the scene also helps preserve evidence of what happened.

opts.t: Tell your supervisor and complete an incident report
opts.fb: Yes. Property damage is reported to your supervisor and in an incident report, even with no injury.

opts.t: Skip the report, since no one was injured
opts.fb: Not quite. Once the situation is stable, you report incidents even when there appears to be no injury.

opts.t: Tidy it all away right now so the workroom looks normal again
opts.fb: Clearing everything right away can remove evidence needed to understand the cause and prevent a repeat.

questions.fb: Respond to injuries, protect the scene, then tell your supervisor and report, even when nobody is hurt.
questions.src: Working Safely 2023 — Slides 34 and 36, In case of an incident; What else should be reported?

questions.q: You strained your back moving workshop tables. You told your supervisor and filed an incident report. Your doctor has sent you to physiotherapy, and you missed Monday. What about WCB?

opts.t: Nothing more. The university reports it to WCB for you
opts.fb: The university does notify WCB, but you also report to WCB yourself when you need treatment beyond first aid or miss time.

opts.t: Report it to WCB yourself as soon as you can
opts.fb: Right. After reporting to your employer, you report to WCB as quickly as possible when treatment goes beyond first aid or you miss work.

opts.t: Wait a few weeks to see if physio fixes it first
opts.fb: Waiting isn't the guidance. Report to WCB as quickly as possible after reporting to your employer.

questions.src: Working Safely 2023 — Slide 43, Workers' Compensation Board
questions.note: SME: confirm wording on how workers report to WCB (e.g., WCB worker report form/channel) if the bank should name it; source names no channel.

questions.q: You've each already told your supervisor and reported these work injuries. In which cases should you also report to WCB? Select all that apply.

opts.t: Ji-woo needed stitches at a clinic for a cut from a paper trimmer
opts.fb: Yes. Stitches at a clinic go beyond first aid, so she reports to WCB.

opts.t: Omar went home after a fall and missed the rest of his shift
opts.fb: Yes. Missed time from work is a reason to report to WCB.

opts.t: Tess isn't sure whether her sore wrist needs more than first aid
opts.fb: Yes. The guidance is simple: unsure? Report it.

opts.t: Ben covered a paper cut with a bandage from the first aid kit and kept working
opts.fb: First aid only, with no missed time, doesn't meet the WCB reporting triggers in the course. Still report the incident to your supervisor.

questions.fb: Report to WCB after reporting to your employer if you need treatment beyond first aid or miss work. Unsure? Report it.

questions.q: You've been off work after an injury with a WCB claim. You're feeling better and want to talk about coming back. Who do you contact?

opts.t: Health, Safety and Environment (HSE), at hse.info@ualberta.ca
opts.fb: HSE helps with safety questions and processes, but return to work after an injury goes to Employee Recovery and Return to Work.

opts.t: Employee Recovery and Return to Work (recovery@ualberta.ca)
opts.fb: Right. The course directs you to the U of A Employee Recovery and Return to Work team at recovery@ualberta.ca.

opts.t: The Control Centre at 780-492-5555, for HSE On Call

questions.q: On Wednesday morning, a toner cartridge splits while you're changing it, scattering black powder across the workroom floor. What do you do?

opts.t: Sweep it up with a dustpan yourself and mention it if anyone asks
opts.fb: Before cleaning, check what the product is and how to clean it up safely. Spills are also reported right away, not only if asked.

opts.t: Check its SDS for how to clean it up, then report it right away
opts.fb: Right. For a spill, find out what it is, check the Safety Data Sheet (SDS) for how to clean it up, and report it immediately.

opts.t: Leave it for the evening cleaning staff to deal with tonight
opts.fb: Leaving a spill for others to discover risks someone walking through it, and it still needs to be reported.

questions.q: Your manager asks you to lead a project team of two coordinators for six months, assigning their daily work. You've already completed Working Safely. What safety training applies now?

opts.t: Nothing new, since Working Safely covers all staff
opts.fb: Working Safely is for workers who don't direct others. Once you direct someone's work, you're considered a supervisor.

opts.t: Supervisor safety training, because you'll be directing others
opts.fb: Right. Directing the activities of a worker is enough to make you a supervisor, and supervisors must complete supervisor safety training.

opts.t: Supervisor training, but only if your job title changes
opts.fb: Your title doesn't decide it. Team leads and people directing others' work count as supervisors even without the word in their title.

questions.src: Working Safely 2023 — Slides 14, 32 and 55, What is a Supervisor?; You the employee; Lead by example

questions.q: Nadia starts as a program coordinator in OD next week. She won't supervise anyone. Which safety training must she complete?

opts.t: Working Safely and Workplace Violence and Harassment Prevention
opts.fb: Right. Both are mandated for all U of A employees.

opts.t: Working Safely only, because she won't be working in a lab or shop
opts.fb: Working Safely isn't the only mandated course. All employees also complete Workplace Violence and Harassment Prevention.

opts.t: Supervising Safely, which all new staff take first

opts.fb: The course says OD doesn't keep copies long term, so save your own.

opts.t: Save a copy and make sure your supervisor has your record

opts.t: Plan to retake it soon, since it's valid for three years
opts.fb: Right. Your certificate is valid for three years, so plan to renew it before it lapses.

opts.t: Retake it only if your duties change

questions.q: A contractor is replacing ceiling tiles in your suite's hallway. Their ladder narrows the route to the kitchenette, and dust is drifting onto nearby desks. What do you do?

opts.t: Tell your supervisor that something appears unsafe
opts.fb: Right. When working near contractors, contact your supervisor if something appears unsafe.

opts.t: Move the ladder aside yourself to clear the route
opts.fb: Moving a contractor's equipment can create new hazards for them. Respect their work space and raise the concern.

opts.t: Work around it, since contractor sites are their concern
opts.fb: Safety is shared. Hazards that affect both parties should be communicated, starting with your supervisor.

questions.src: Working Safely 2023 — Slide 53, Working with Contractors

questions.q: Facilities tells your team that contractors will be rewiring part of your floor for two weeks. You're running a 30-person workshop there on Thursday. What's your part? Select all that apply.

opts.t: Tell the contractors about Thursday's workshop
opts.fb: Yes. Communicate the hazards and activities that affect both parties.

opts.t: Attend the contractor's site orientation if you're asked to
opts.fb: Yes. Attend the contractor's site orientation, if required.

opts.t: Contact your supervisor if something in their area looks unsafe
opts.fb: Yes. That's the first step when something appears unsafe.

opts.t: Leave every bit of safety communication to the contractor's foreman
opts.fb: Hazards have to be communicated in both directions, to and from the contractor.

opts.t: Use their work zone as a shortcut while they're on break
opts.fb: Be aware of each other's work space. A work zone is still a hazard area when the crew steps away.

questions.fb: Near contractors: raise unsafe conditions with your supervisor, share hazards both ways, respect their space, and attend orientation if required.

questions.q: Most Fridays you're the only person in the OD suite, and lately you've felt uneasy being there alone. What's a reasonable next step?

opts.t: Treat it as a personal preference and manage it on your own
opts.fb: Working alone is a recognized psychological hazard, not just a matter of personal preference.

opts.t: Raise it with your supervisor so the risk can be assessed
opts.fb: Right. Like physical hazards, psychological hazards such as working alone should be identified, assessed and mitigated.

opts.t: Wait to mention it until something actually goes wrong
opts.fb: Hazard management is about acting before harm happens, by identifying and assessing risks early.

opts.t: Tell your supervisor you're fatigued so plans can change
opts.fb: Right. Treat fatigue as a hazard: raise it so the risk can be assessed and controlled.

opts.t: Have an extra coffee and say nothing to the team

questions.title: Desk to muster point
questions.q: The fire alarm sounds while you're on a call at your desk. Put your evacuation in order. One step doesn't belong.

steps: End your call, close drawers and cabinets, and grab your keys, wallet, coat and safe shoes
Walk to the nearest emergency stairwell (never an elevator or escalator)
If the stairwell door beeps and stays shut, keep holding the push bar for 15 seconds
Go down to the main floor and leave by the exit there (pull the blue pull station to release the lock)
Go to the muster point: the upper platform of the Bay/Enterprise Square LRT station (103 Street entrance)
Wait there until you see the All Clear signs and hear the public address (PA) announcement
order.distractor: Save your open files and shut down your computer
order.fb: Desk to All Clear in six steps. Saving files and shutting down isn't part of the procedure and costs time. The stairs continue to the concourse, but you leave at the main floor, because roll shutters close the LRT entrance and the pedway during an alarm.

questions.title: If you find a fire

Pull the nearest fire alarm
Call 911 with the address (10230 Jasper Avenue) and where the fire is
Evacuate by the stairs
order.distractor: Call ESQ Security and let them decide whether to pull the alarm

questions.title: The box on the high shelf

cards.t: The exit sign light in your stairwell is out.

Stay on the line until the dispatcher hangs up
Call ESQ Security at 780-428-1541: tell them an ambulance is coming and exactly where you are
Once the situation is stable, tell your supervisor and submit a U of A incident report
order.distractor: Put the dispatcher on hold while you quickly ring Security on the same phone
order.fb: 911 gets the ambulance moving. Security then brings first aid and an AED, holds an elevator, and meets paramedics at the street. Don't put 911 on hold: finish that call first. Reporting comes once things are stable.

questions.title: Report it or not?
questions.q: Sort each event. Does it need a U of A incident report (and a word with your supervisor)?

cards.t: A colleague nearly hits her head on a newly installed light. "Nobody got hurt," she says.
cards.fb: It's a near miss. Near misses are incidents, and the new fixture should also trigger a hazard assessment.

cards.t: You're about to hang a banner and notice one of the ladder steps is really loose.
cards.fb: A broken ladder is unstable. Tell your supervisor and find another way to get the job done.

cards.t: You trip over a box in the hallway. You're not hurt and nothing is damaged.
cards.fb: Report it once things are stable, even when there's no injury or damage.

cards.t: A box slides off a shelf and lands where you were standing a second ago.
cards.fb: A close call is a near miss. Reporting it gets the hazard fixed before someone gets hurt.

cards.t: A coat rack tips over in the workroom and cracks a colleague's monitor. Nobody is hurt.
cards.fb: Property damage is reported to your supervisor and in an incident report.

cards.t: A visitor shouts and swears at you at the service desk, then leaves. You're shaken but not hurt.
cards.fb: Prompt reporting of all incidents, including harassment and abuse, helps everyone stay safe.

cards.t: Someone followed you and blocked your way outside ESQ. Police non-emergency has handled it.
cards.fb: Once the authorities have responded, still submit a U of A incident report so the U of A can follow up.

cards.t: Your team's planned fire drill went smoothly.
cards.fb: A planned drill that went as intended isn't an incident.

cards.t: On your way in, someone asks for change. You say "Sorry, not today," and they move on.
cards.fb: Nothing unsafe happened. Report it if someone follows you, blocks you or you feel threatened.

questions.title: Respond, report, recover
questions.q: During workshop setup, a colleague trips over a stack of boxes and cuts her arm. Put the steps in order, from the first response to getting back to normal. One step doesn't belong.

steps: Respond to the injury right away: get first aid or medical help as needed
Protect the scene: keep people clear so no one else gets hurt, and leave things where they are
Once the situation is stable, tell your supervisor
Report it on the U of A incident report form (for a serious or potentially serious incident, also call the Control Centre at 780-492-5555 and ask for HSE On Call)
Recover: follow your unit's operational continuity plan, and report any damage to your supervisor
order.distractor: Tidy everything away right away so the room looks normal before participants arrive
order.fb: Respond first, then protect the scene to prevent a second incident and preserve evidence. Once things are stable, tell your supervisor and report, even if nobody was hurt. Recovery means getting back to work safely and reporting damage. Clearing up straight away can remove the evidence needed to prevent a repeat.

questions.src: Working Safely 2023 — Slide 34, In case of an incident; Slide 35, Serious and potentially serious incidents; Slide 48, What happens after an emergency?
questions.note: Calm framing: the cut is minor and is being bandaged in the source item (incidents-30/31). The Working Safely 'recovery' step is written for emergencies; SME: confirm it's fine to apply it to an incident. At ESQ, 'medical help' means 911 first, then ESQ Security; consider saying so in feedback.

questions.title: Refusing dangerous work
questions.q: Malik asks you to climb a storage shelving unit that sways when you touch it, and you believe a fall could seriously hurt you. Put the work refusal steps in order. One step doesn't belong.

steps: Tell Malik your concern and work with him to make the work safer
If you can't resolve it together, confirm with Malik that you're officially refusing for safety reasons
Call the Control Centre (780-492-5555) and ask for the HSE officer on call
Malik investigates while you keep your regular pay, and you can't be disciplined for refusing
Malik gives you a report explaining what was done about the danger
If you think the danger still hasn't been corrected, contact HSE at hse.info@ualberta.ca
order.distractor: Do the task quickly while a coworker holds the shelving unit steady
order.fb: A work refusal is a last resort: start by working with your supervisor. If you refuse, HSE helps you through the process, your pay continues and you're protected from discipline. Never do work you believe is a serious and immediate threat.

questions.title: Who do I call? Downtown edition
questions.q: Sort each situation around ESQ by the first contact you'd use.

cards.t: On the 103 Street sidewalk, someone is lying unconscious and won't respond.
cards.fb: It's a medical emergency. Call 911 and give the nearest intersection.

cards.t: Someone slumped outside is barely breathing. You think it's an overdose.
cards.fb: Call 911, then get a naloxone kit from the ESQ Security desk (main floor, by the elevators), or ask someone to.

cards.t: A person by the Jasper Avenue doors is very intoxicated and confused, but calm and breathing normally.
cards.fb: The 24/7 Crisis Diversion team is set up for this. If the person becomes unresponsive, call 911.

cards.t: Near the bike racks, someone is using illegal drugs. No one is in danger.
cards.fb: Call 780-423-4567 (or #377 from a cell). You can also report through Crime Stoppers.

cards.t: Someone asking for money follows you and blocks your way. You feel intimidated.
cards.fb: Get to a safe place first, then report aggressive panhandling. Call 911 if it's an emergency.

cards.t: On the LRT platform under ESQ, a rider is shouting threats at other passengers. Nobody is hurt.
cards.fb: The LRT is City jurisdiction. Call or text ETS. If anyone is in danger, call 911.

cards.t: It's 9:30 PM and dark. Your car is a block away and you'd rather not walk alone.
cards.fb: Ask for a Safe Walk: free within two blocks of ESQ, ideally booked about an hour ahead.

cards.t: It's 8:40 PM. You checked in earlier, the alarm sounded, and you're out at the muster point.
cards.fb: Tell Security you're out, or responders may search the building for you.

cards.t: After hours, someone you don't recognize slips in behind you at the door.
cards.fb: Don't confront them. Call Security and describe them.

cards.t: A colleague collapses and isn't responding.

cards.t: A caller on your desk line says there's a bomb in the building.

cards.t: Water is pooling under the kitchen sink.
cards.fb: Not 911. Report floods to ClikFix with your name and location.

cards.t: The exit sign light in your stairwell is out.
cards.fb: Not Security. Unsafe building conditions go to ClikFix.

cards.t: A contractor is smoking in a stairwell inside ESQ.
cards.fb: Not ClikFix. Someone smoking onsite is reported to Security.

cards.t: An unattended bag in the concourse looks suspicious.

cards.t: From your window, you see what looks like a funnel cloud forming.

cards.fb: Not ESQ Security: the LRT is City jurisdiction. Call or text ETS. If anyone is in danger, call 911.

cards.t: Near the bike racks, someone is using illegal drugs. No one is in danger.

cards.t: You've told Security about a suspicious box. Who's your next call?
