questions.title: Two helpers, one plan
questions.q: Work through the alarm with Priya. Choose what you do at each point.

branching.setup: Tuesday · 10:40 AM. A few weeks ago, Priya told her manager she'd need help on the stairs for a while. The Floor Warden set up a plan and asked you and Tomás to be her two helpers. You're on a call at your desk across the floor when the fire alarm sounds.

nodes.prompt: The alarm is sounding. What do you do?

choices.t: End your call, grab your keys, wallet and coat, and go to Priya
choices.consequence: Priya has ended her own call and has her coat. Tomás arrives a moment after you. The plan works because everyone knows their part before an alarm.

choices.t: Head for the nearest stairwell and tell the Floor Warden where Priya is on your way
choices.consequence: The Floor Warden, in a red cap and vest, reminds you that Priya is waiting for her two helpers. You turn back and join her and Tomás. Helpers go to the person first.

choices.t: Text Priya to meet you at the stairwell
choices.consequence: Priya replies that she'll wait at her desk for you both, as planned. Stairwells are for people going down, so you go to her, and Tomás joins you.

nodes.prompt: The three of you are together. A colleague hurrying past says, "The elevator's right there. Take her down before it shuts off." What do you do?

choices.t: Go with Priya and Tomás to the elevator lobby on your floor and wait there
choices.consequence: The elevator lobby is the designated area on every floor, marked with the blue wheelchair symbol. Emergency responders come there.

choices.t: Wait for the crowd to thin, then help her down the stairwell one step at a time
choices.consequence: Tomás points out that this puts you both at risk in a busy stairwell. You settle in the elevator lobby instead, where responders come.

choices.t: Press the elevator button and try to get down quickly
choices.consequence: During an alarm, elevators return to the main floor and stop, so it won't come. The elevator lobby itself is the safe place to wait. You stay there together.

nodes.prompt: The Floor Warden has checked the floor, seen the three of you in the lobby, and left by the stairs. The floor is quiet now. What do you do?

choices.t: Stay with Priya until emergency responders arrive or Security gives the All Clear
choices.consequence: The Floor Warden reports to Security that you're there, so responders know exactly where to find you. There's no time limit on waiting.

choices.t: Now that the stairwell is empty, help her down
choices.consequence: People who need help on the stairs don't self-evacuate, even on a quiet stairwell. You stay put. Responders know you're in the lobby.

choices.t: Go down yourself to tell Security the three of you are up here
choices.consequence: The Floor Warden is already reporting your location to Security, and Priya needs both helpers with her. You stay in the lobby with her and Tomás.

branching.resolution: Security gives the All Clear and the PA announcement follows. The three of you head back to your desks, and the afternoon carries on. At 4:30, Priya waves on her way out, coat on, heading home.

questions.src: ESQ Emergency Procedures 2025 — Individuals with Mobility Restrictions; Floor Wardens; Alarm Response (Tenants); ESQ Ready lesson content — Help a teammate out
questions.note: The story never asks the learner to name, record or disclose why Priya needs help; she spoke to her manager herself, and helpers are told only that she needs help on stairs. The after-hours version (mobility-06, mobility-07: call 911, help station) is practised in late-f01. SME: confirm that a helper should not leave to report to Security when the Floor Warden has already reported (based on mobility-05 feedback).

questions.title: The coffee code
questions.q: A visitor is making you uneasy. Choose what you do at each point.

branching.setup: Thursday · 2:10 PM. You're at the front desk of your suite, 2-334. A visitor waiting for a colleague has started pacing. He's getting agitated and watching you closely. You pick up the phone and call ESQ Security at 780-428-1541.

nodes.prompt: Security answers. The visitor can hear you. What do you say?

choices.t: "Can you bring me a coffee? I'm in 2-334."
choices.consequence: Phrase first, then your suite. Security sends an officer right away and puts others on standby, and the visitor hears only a coffee order.

choices.t: "Hi, I'm in 2-334. Can you bring me a coffee?"
choices.consequence: Close, but the order matters. You say it again with the phrase first: "Can you bring me a coffee? I'm in 2-334." Now Security knows to record the location that follows.

choices.t: "Hi, it's me. Could someone come up when they have a minute?"
choices.consequence: That sounds routine, and Security has no location. You call back and say, "Can you bring me a coffee? I'm in 2-334."

nodes.prompt: Security has the phrase and your suite. The visitor is still close by. Do you add anything?

choices.t: Add where you are in the suite only if you can do it calmly, then end the call
choices.consequence: Your suite number was the essential part. A detail like "by the printers at the back" helps only if it won't raise suspicion. An officer is on the way.

choices.t: Describe the visitor and what he's doing
choices.consequence: Describing him out loud could escalate things. You stop there and end the call. Officers come to you; your suite number is what they need.

choices.t: Give your name and department so they can log the call
choices.consequence: Helpful in other calls, but it won't speed up the officer. Security already has what matters: the phrase and your suite.

nodes.prompt: Before the officer arrives, the visitor follows your coworker into the hallway, shouting threats and stepping closer to her. What do you do?

choices.t: Get away, warn others, get into a meeting room, lock and block the door, then call 911 and ESQ Security
choices.consequence: Distance and a barrier come first. Your coworker moves away too and joins you. Once the door is locked and blocked, you make the calls.

choices.t: Step between them and try to calm him down
choices.consequence: Confronting a violent person puts you at risk. You step back, tell your coworker to come with you, and get into a meeting room. Then you lock the door and call 911 and Security.

choices.t: Stay back and record it on your phone as evidence
choices.consequence: Staying nearby keeps you at risk. You put the phone away, leave with your coworker, lock and block a meeting-room door, and call 911 and Security. Details can be reported afterward.

branching.resolution: The officer arrives and takes over, and Security lets you know when it's safe to come out. Your supervisor checks in with you both. Just after five, you and your coworker walk out together and head home.

questions.src: ESQ Emergency Procedures 2025 — Important Telephone Numbers; Security Safety Phrase; Violent Persons Procedures; ESQ Ready lesson content — The coffee code
questions.note: Duress phrase kept exactly as "Can you bring me a coffee?". Suite 2-334 is the example used in security-02 and the app; swap for the learner's suite if needed. SME: security-02 feedback says Security "puts other staff on standby" while the app card says "other officers"; this story says "others" until confirmed. Possible-gunfire items (security-06, security-07) are left out of the story to keep the tone calm; they stay as choice items. "Security lets you know when it's safe" and the supervisor check-in in the resolution are not stated in the procedures; confirm or trim.

questions.title: Safe to speak up
questions.q: A colleague raises a concern at the Monday check-in. Choose what you do at each point.

branching.setup: Monday · 9:30 AM. Your team is reviewing last Friday's workshop. Jae, who joined the team in the fall, says, "I think the registration link might be sending some people to the wrong form." A colleague sighs, "Here we go again." Jae goes quiet.

nodes.prompt: The room is quiet. What do you do?

choices.t: Say you'd like to hear more, and ask Jae to go on
choices.consequence: Jae picks up again and explains what they noticed. A small act like this keeps safe voice alive in the room.

choices.t: Let the meeting move on, and talk to Jae afterwards
choices.consequence: Jae appreciates it, but the team never hears the concern, and the sigh goes unanswered. You ask Jae if you can bring it back to the group before the meeting ends, and Jae agrees.

choices.t: Stay out of it; it's the lead's meeting
choices.consequence: The lead moves to the next item. Leaders matter, but culture is shaped by everyone's behaviour. You raise your hand and ask Jae to finish the point.

nodes.prompt: As Jae explains, you realize the link is one you set up. About 12 people were sent to the wrong form. What do you do?

choices.t: Say it's your link, and say how you'll fix it
choices.consequence: The lead thanks you both. Naming your own mistake calmly makes it easier for the next person to raise theirs.

choices.t: Stay quiet and fix it yourself after the meeting
choices.consequence: The link gets fixed, but the team can't learn from it, and Jae is left wondering if they were heard. You email the team that afternoon to say it was your link and what you changed.

choices.t: Wait to see whether anyone is actually affected
choices.consequence: Waiting lets the problem grow and keeps it hidden. Before the meeting wraps up, you say it was your link and that you'll fix it today.

nodes.prompt: Later, a Teams thread about how to fix the form turns sarcastic between you and the colleague who sighed. What do you do?

choices.t: Suggest a quick call and keep it to the ideas
choices.consequence: Ten minutes on a call sorts out the fix. Treating differences as a discussion, not a battle, keeps the team working together.

choices.t: Reply in the same tone so they see how it feels
choices.consequence: The thread gets sharper and others go quiet. You step back and suggest a quick call about the fix instead.

choices.t: Drop out of the thread and let others decide
choices.consequence: The tension stays unresolved, and the fix stalls. You message your colleague and suggest a quick call to sort it out.

branching.resolution: The form is fixed by Tuesday, and the 12 people get a corrected link. At the next check-in, Jae raises a small scheduling issue without starting with "Sorry." At the end of the day, Jae says "See you tomorrow" and heads home.

questions.src: Psychologically Safe Workplaces — Video takeaways 2 (Organizational Culture) and 4 (Civility & Respect); A Culture of Care — Safety definitions (psychological safety)
questions.note: Combines the Jae (psych-23), registration-link (psych-22) and Teams-thread (psych-26) situations into one story; psych-15's "thank them and invite them to raise things" logic appears in node 2's good outcome. Choices are all staff-level (no supervisor actions). Consequence details (lead thanks you, corrected link by Tuesday) are illustrative story text, not source facts.

questions.title: The late alarm
questions.q: You're working late with Raj. Choose what you do at each point.

branching.setup: Wednesday · 7:00 PM. You and Raj are the last two from your team on the 3rd floor. You checked in with ESQ Security at 5:00 and said you'd leave at 7:00. Raj is on crutches this month, and he has already told his manager he'd need help on the stairs. You both need about another hour.

nodes.prompt: It's 7:00, the time you said you'd leave. What do you do?

choices.t: Call Security at 780-428-1541 to update your departure time
choices.consequence: Security updates its record. Their list now matches where you really are.

choices.t: Nothing. Security checks on you every hour anyway
choices.consequence: Hourly checks don't replace an update. You call Security a few minutes later with your new time.

choices.t: Plan to sign the logbook again on your way out
choices.consequence: That would be too late if something happened before then. You call Security now with the change.

nodes.prompt: 7:30 PM. The fire alarm sounds. Raj can't manage the stairs. What do the two of you do?

choices.t: Go together to the 3rd-floor elevator lobby and call 911 with your floor and exact location
choices.consequence: The elevator lobby is the mobility designated area on every floor, and responders come there. After hours there may be no Floor Warden to report you, so you call. If a phone isn't handy, a help station goes straight to Security.

choices.t: Help Raj down the stairwell one step at a time
choices.consequence: It's risky for you both. Raj suggests the elevator lobby instead. You go there together and call 911 with your floor and location.

choices.t: Leave Raj at his desk and go down to get Security
choices.consequence: Responders look for people in the elevator lobby, not at desks. You go back, walk with Raj to the lobby, and call 911 from there.

nodes.prompt: Responders help Raj out, and you both reach the muster point on the upper LRT platform. You're cold and want to go home. What do you do first?

choices.t: Tell Security that you're both out of the building
choices.consequence: You checked in, so Security has you on its list. Now they know not to search for you.

choices.t: Head home. Security can see your names in the logbook
choices.consequence: That's the issue: Security still thinks you're inside. You turn back and let them know you're both out.

choices.t: Text your manager and leave
choices.consequence: Your manager isn't tracking who's inside tonight; Security is. You find a Security officer and tell them you're both out.

branching.resolution: Security crosses you both off its list and gives the All Clear a little later. Raj's ride pulls up nearby, and you both head home.

questions.src: ESQ Emergency Procedures 2025 — Working After Hours; Individuals with Mobility Restrictions, After Hours Alarm Response; ESQ Ready lesson content — Working late
questions.note: Adapted from case-late: its decisions 1 and 3 are kept; its help-station decision is folded into the node 2 consequence so the first decision can practise late-03 (updating your departure time). If the case-late case should remain unchanged in the Final, this story overlaps it; consider using one or the other. SME: "Security crosses you off its list" is inferred from "report to Security so nobody searches for you."

cases.title: Smoke in the copy room
cases.q: Final challenge. Choose what you do at each point.

branching.setup: Tuesday · 2:15 PM. Walking past the copy room, you smell smoke and see a small flame in the recycling bin. No one else is in the room.

nodes.prompt: What do you do first?

choices.t: Leave the room, warn people nearby, and close the door behind you
choices.consequence: A closed door helps hold back fire and smoke. Two colleagues nearby head for the stairs.

choices.t: Grab the extinguisher in the hallway, even though you've never been trained
choices.consequence: Never risk your safety on a fire you aren't trained to fight. You put the extinguisher back, leave, warn people, and close the door.

choices.t: Call Security and wait for them to decide
choices.consequence: Waiting costs time. You leave the room, warn people nearby, and close the door. Then you raise the alarm.

nodes.prompt: The door is closed. There's a pull station beside the stairwell. What next?

choices.t: Pull the alarm, then call 911 and evacuate by the stairs
choices.consequence: The alarm tells everyone to get out. You give 911 the address, 10230 Jasper Avenue, and where the fire is.

choices.t: Call 911, but don't pull the alarm so you don't cause panic
choices.consequence: The alarm is how everyone else learns to get out. You pull it, then head for the stairs.

choices.t: Take the escalator down to the main floor to report it
choices.consequence: In an alarm, use an emergency stairwell, not the escalators or elevators. You pull the alarm and take the stairs, calling 911 on the way.

nodes.prompt: In the stairwell, a colleague's foot slips on a step. She catches the rail and isn't hurt, and you all get out. After the All Clear, what else needs to happen?

choices.t: Tell your supervisor and file a U of A incident report about the slip
choices.consequence: An unplanned event that could have caused an injury is an incident, even during an emergency. The report helps fix whatever caused the slip.

choices.t: Nothing. It happened during an evacuation, and she's fine
choices.consequence: It still counts. Any unplanned event that caused, or could have caused, an injury gets reported. You tell your supervisor and file the report.

choices.t: Only report it if she ends up missing work
choices.consequence: Waiting to see how it turns out isn't the rule. You tell your supervisor and report it that afternoon.

branching.resolution: The fire crew confirms the fire was contained to the bin, and Security gives the All Clear. Your supervisor thanks you for the report. Later, you shut down your computer and head home.

cases.src: ESQ Ready lesson content — If you discover a fire; ESQ Emergency Procedures 2025 — Alarm Response (Tenants); Working Safely (U of A HSE) — In case of an incident
cases.note: SME: the original case had the colleague twist her ankle in the stairwell. To meet the calm-tone constraint (no injuries), it's now a slip where she catches the rail and isn't hurt. The correct decision (tell your supervisor and file an incident report) is unchanged, since near misses are reportable (incidents-02, alerts-07). Case-level tier/kind were not in the bank; set to A/decide from fire-01..04. "The fire crew confirms the fire was contained" in the resolution is story text, not a source fact.

cases.title: After hours in the lunchroom
cases.q: Final challenge. Choose what you do at each point.

branching.setup: Thursday · 6:45 PM. You've checked in with ESQ Security for the evening. In the staff lunchroom, a colleague collapses and isn't responding.

nodes.prompt: Who do you call first?

choices.t: 911, to request an ambulance
choices.consequence: Every minute counts, and paramedics are dispatched. Next, you'll call ESQ Security at 780-428-1541.

choices.t: ESQ Security, so they can decide whether to call 911
choices.consequence: Security can help, but 911 comes first. You end the call and dial 911 straight away.

choices.t: Your supervisor
choices.consequence: Your supervisor can hear about it afterwards. You hang up and call 911 first.

nodes.prompt: The 911 dispatcher is still asking questions, and you want to call Security now. What do you do?

choices.t: Stay on the line until the dispatcher hangs up, then call Security
choices.consequence: The dispatcher may need more details or give you instructions. You follow them until the call ends.

choices.t: Hang up so you can call Security straight away
choices.consequence: The dispatcher may have life-saving instructions. You call 911 back and stay on until they end the call.

choices.t: Put 911 on hold and call Security
choices.consequence: Don't put 911 on hold. You come back to the dispatcher and finish that call first.

nodes.prompt: Now you call ESQ Security at 780-428-1541. What do you tell them?

choices.t: That an ambulance is coming, and exactly where you are
choices.consequence: Security brings first aid and an AED, holds an elevator, and meets the paramedics at the street.

choices.t: Just your name, so they can log the call
choices.consequence: The officer needs more. You add that an ambulance is coming and that you're in the staff lunchroom, so they can bring the AED and guide paramedics.

choices.t: Ask them to call 911 again to be sure
choices.consequence: 911 is already coming. You tell the officer that, and give your exact location.

branching.resolution: Paramedics arrive with a Security officer and take over. You tell your supervisor what happened. Before you leave, you let Security know you're heading out, and you head home.

cases.src: ESQ Emergency Procedures 2025 — Medical Emergency Procedures; ESQ Ready lesson content — First on scene
cases.note: Case-level tier/kind were not in the bank; set to A/do from medical-01/03/09. Node 3 good outcome quotes the case feedback (Security brings first aid and an AED, holds an elevator, meets paramedics). The check-out to Security in the resolution reflects the after-hours check-in practice.

cases.title: The cord, again
cases.q: Final challenge. Choose what you do at each point.

branching.setup: Monday · 10:05 AM. At the team check-in, the new coordinator says quietly, "Sorry, it's probably just me, but I tripped on the printer cord again this morning." Someone laughs.

nodes.prompt: How do you respond in the meeting?

choices.t: Thank her for raising it, and say the team should fix it today
choices.consequence: The laughter stops, and someone offers to help. Thanking people who speak up, then acting, keeps speaking up safe.

choices.t: Laugh along so she doesn't feel awkward
choices.consequence: She looks down and says nothing more. Laughter can feel like humiliation. You add, "Thanks for raising it. Let's fix it today."

choices.t: Say nothing. It's the lead's meeting
choices.consequence: The meeting moves on, and silence reads as dismissal. Before the next item, you thank her and suggest fixing it today.

nodes.prompt: After the meeting, which fix do you push for first?

choices.t: Move the printer or reroute the cord so it no longer crosses the walkway
choices.consequence: That removes the hazard: the strongest control. Next week, you check that it's still clear.

choices.t: Tape a "Watch your step" sign by the cord
choices.consequence: Signs rely on people noticing them. You suggest moving the printer instead, so the cord no longer crosses the walkway.

choices.t: Remind everyone to be careful near the printer
choices.consequence: Reminders are the weakest kind of fix. You suggest rerouting the cord so the hazard is gone.

nodes.prompt: She wasn't hurt either time. Does the trip need reporting?

choices.t: Yes. Tell your supervisor and file a near-miss report today
choices.consequence: Near misses are incidents, and reports get hazards fixed before someone is hurt.

choices.t: No. Nobody got hurt
choices.consequence: Near misses count, injury or not. You tell your supervisor and file the report that day.

choices.t: Only if it happens a third time
choices.consequence: Two trips already show the hazard is real. You tell your supervisor and file the report today.

branching.resolution: By Tuesday, the printer sits against the wall and the walkway is clear. At the next check-in, the coordinator raises another small issue without apologizing first. At five, she grabs her coat and heads home.

cases.src: Psychologically Safe Workplaces — Video takeaway 2 (Organizational Culture); Working Safely (U of A HSE) — Hierarchy of controls; In case of an incident
cases.note: Case-level tier/kind were not in the bank; set to B/decide (mixed C psych and B hazmgmt/incidents items). Node 2 good outcome adds "check that it's still clear" from the case feedback ("then check that it worked", hazmgmt-07).

cases.title: The late alarm
cases.q: Choose what you do at each point.

branching.setup: Wednesday · 7:30 PM. You and Raj are the last two from your team still working on the 3rd floor. You checked in with ESQ Security at 5:00. Raj is on crutches this month. The fire alarm sounds.

nodes.prompt: Raj can't manage the stairs. What do the two of you do?

choices.t: Go together to the 3rd-floor elevator lobby and call 911 with your floor and exact location
choices.consequence: Right. The elevator lobby is the mobility designated area on every floor, and emergency responders come there. After hours there may be no Floor Warden to report you, so call.

choices.t: Help Raj down the stairwell one step at a time
choices.consequence: Risky for both of you, and it slows everyone else in the stairwell. Wait in the elevator lobby, where responders come.

choices.t: Leave Raj at his desk and run down to get Security
choices.consequence: Responders look for people in the elevator lobby, not at desks. Stay together and call.

nodes.prompt: While you wait in the elevator lobby, your phone dies. How do you reach Security?

choices.t: Use a help station to call Security
choices.consequence: Help stations go straight to the Security desk. Stay in the elevator lobby until you're rescued or Security gives the All Clear.

choices.t: Leave Raj and walk down to the Security desk
choices.consequence: Stay with Raj. A help station reaches Security without leaving him alone.

choices.t: Take Raj back to his desk to use his phone
choices.consequence: Stay in the elevator lobby, where responders will look for you. Use a help station.

nodes.prompt: Responders help Raj out, and you both reach the muster point. You're cold and want to go home. What do you do first?

choices.t: Tell Security you're both out of the building
choices.consequence: You checked in, so Security has you on its list. Otherwise responders may search the building for you.

choices.t: Go home. The alarm is someone else's problem now
choices.consequence: Security still thinks you're inside, so responders may go looking for you.

choices.t: Text your manager and leave
choices.consequence: Your manager isn't tracking who's inside tonight. Security is. Tell them you're out.
